The improved power may not stick around since Lopez still didn't consistently make hard contact, but double-digit homers with 20-plus steals is a realistic expectation at this point, though the other counting stats are likely to be limited. Lopez opened 2025 as Miami's primary second baseman but was shifted to shortstop midseason, and his strong defense at both positions will help to keep him in the lineup.

The active career leader in saves (476), Jansen's skills gradually eroded as he progressed through his mid-30s, but the Tigers see enough potential in him at age 38 that they signed him as their presumptive closer. He has saved at least 25 games in each of the past 13 uninterrupted MLB seasons, but 2025 saw him register career worsts in strikeout rate (24.4%), Statcast expected ERA (3.74) and hard-hit rate allowed (44.6%). Jansen is a role-driven, middle-of-your-staff type for fantasy purposes, the promise of save chances in Detroit buoying his value -- so long as he pitches effectively enough to keep the job.

One of 2025's biggest disappointments, Williams simply couldn't get the job done in the ninth for the Yankees. It took him just one month to get removed as their closer, after he surrendered as many earned runs in that time (10) as he had during the entirety of his career-year 2023. His season-ending ERA wound up being nearly three full runs higher than the total over his first six MLB seasons. In Williams' strong defense, however, he had outrageous numbers over the final four months in terms of batting average allowed (.172) and strikeout rate (38.6%) -- and he was done in by a 55.2 LOB% that was lower than any qualified reliever had posted in three years. The Mets, who signed him to serve as their 2026 closer, surely saw this and expect a full rebound. We tend to agree.

A Will Smith won another World Series, but Smith is more than just a funny trivia question. He has been a force at the catching position for fantasy managers these past few seasons, even as he lost some of the volume this past year as the designated hitter spot on the roster was re-occupied by Shohei Ohtani. Smith was on pace to best his 2024 production despite the reduction in plate appearances and also went on to post a career-best batting average in 2025. If anything, one could argue the reduced volume was a good thing for Smith to keep him fresh over the course of a full season under the physical demands of catching. This season should be more of the same for playing time and production with a step back toward his career level for batting average with batted-ball luck coming back to previous norms.

For only the second time in his nine MLB seasons, Pagan seized hold of a closer opportunity and thrived in it, this time setting personal bests with his 56 games finished, 32 saves and 340 fantasy points (eight more than in his other closer year of 2019). A much-improved splitter had a lot to do with it, fueling career bests of a .161 BAA and .507 OPS allowed to lefties. That should ensure Pagan a long ninth-inning leash, though he's one of the greater risk/reward closers based upon his skill set, as an extreme fly baller whose control is only so-so. Draft Pagan in the middle rounds, once the higher-ceiling closers are gone.

Ramirez arrived in Miami three weeks into the season and, as is all the rage these days, saw near-everyday time between catcher and DH to fuel what was the third-most fantasy points by any catcher-eligible player from that point forward. Though he cooled over the season's final three months, batting only .212 with a .633 OPS, his fantasy value was buoyed by his 15 stolen bases over that time. His well-rounded game, and his penchant for contact, gives him a good shot at another top-10 catcher season, if not a step forward in 2026.

The AL’s leading base stealer in both of the last two seasons, Caballero has the look of a single-category, roto-angled standout -- until you look closer. He improved his plate approach and the resulting walk rate (12.7%) last year, demonstrated above-average defense at five different positions (while also appearing in a sixth, in center field) and gave the Yankees reasonable cause to let him push Anthony Volpe for their starting shortstop job this spring. Caballero’s skill set indeed is better suited for roto play, where he’s a strong mid-round pick for his steals, but a standout March could make him a potential breakout candidate.

Glasnow was unable to repeat his overall performance from 2024 when he set a new career high with just 134 innings of work, but did at least post a career-best 3.19 ERA over the 18 starts he made. The ERA was surprising since his walk rate jumped from 6.7 percent to 11.7 percent last season, dropping his normally stellar K-BB to a career-low 17.2 percent. Glasnow was still impossible to hit as the league hit .175 against him last season, which is not surprising since only Freddy Peralta, Jacob deGrom and Max Scherzer have been tougher to hit amongst all starting pitchers in baseball since Glasnow joined the league in 2016. Glasnow has some of the nastiest stuff in baseball, but he also has one of the most fragile bodies as something always breaks down. Expect 120 innings of valuable contributions but not much more.

Regarded as the Royals’ catcher of the future, or at least a catcher/DH partner for Salvador Perez until the latter’s retirement, Jensen has an unusually sound combination of plate discipline and pop -- or at least it’s unusual for a backstop. He received a September cup of coffee with the Royals, hitting three homers with a .941 OPS in his 20 games, and he now figures to grab a similar role with the big club to begin 2026. Jensen has one of the highest ceilings among young catchers, and the promise of DH at-bats boosts his appeal in the runs/RBI categories. If he looks likely to break camp with the team, he could be a top-10 fantasy catcher right from the start.

Misiorowski, one of the game's top prospects, arrived in the majors last June to pitch five no-hit innings in his first career start, and post a 2.81 ERA and 33.7% strikeout rate across his first five. Unfortunately, between his mediocre control and the shin contusion that cost him a 17-day stay on the IL, he couldn't maintain that pace the rest of the way and his ERA ballooned to 5.36 across his final nine starts and one relief appearance. Misiorowski's raw stuff, however, was consistently excellent, and if the Brewers trust him to pitch deeper into games, he could break out in a big way in 2026. There's danger here of overrating him, but among mid-round picks, he carries a lot of upside.

The No. 2 overall pick in the 2024 Draft, Burns soared to the majors after only 13 minor-league starts, then used his 98.7-mph fastball and filthy slider to post four games of double-digit strikeouts in his first eight, as well as a 37.7% K rate over that time. While he had some issues with lefties and missed time due to a flexor strain, he did return to make five solid relief appearances and figures to make the Reds' rotation out of spring training. Burns has some work to do on improving a pitch to use against lefties, and he's a little too fly ball-oriented to avoid issues with homers in Great American Ball Park, but he's one of the most intriguing breakthrough candidates among pitchers. He's a dynasty league building block and a mid-round target in redraft formats.

Traded from Anaheim in November, Ward will be part of the new-look Orioles under new skipper Craig Albernaz in 2026. Ward's tenure with the Angels culminated in career highs in home runs (36) and RBI (103) last season, with the outfielder ranking in the top six in the AL in both categories, after previously topping out at 25 homers and 75 RBI in 2024. The right-handed slugger continues to mash lefties, and he at least hits for power against same-side arms if not for batting average. Ward added to his walk rate last season and his offensive contributions more than made up for his defensive limitations. Now 32, Ward should be in position to knock in the runners Pete Alonso leaves on base while batting in the middle of the everyday lineup in Baltimore.

Busch is coming off a tremendous sophomore season which saw him flex his power to another level while improving his strikeout rate five full percentage points. Busch hit 30 of his 34 homers against righties and was quite neutralized by lefties all season, and he found road parks to be more conducive to his homers with 21 of the 34 coming away from Wrigley Field. Busch may also be one of the few players to hit 30 or more home runs in a season during which his most common position in the batting order was leadoff, as he led off for the Cubs in 52 contests last season. Should that usage continue, Busch is likely to score more runs than he drives in, but he did still manage 90 RBI last season. If he and Ian Happ flip in the projected lineup around Nico Hoerner, Busch could drive in 100-plus.

Despite Woodruff recently missing the better part of two years and ending 2025 back on the injured list with a lat strain, Milwaukee extended him the qualifying offer for 2026, which speaks to just how well he pitched when available last season. After his recovery from 2023 shoulder surgery was set back several times, Woodruff finally returned with five quality starts in his first six outings before enduring a couple hiccups in August. His xBA and xERA were both among the very best in baseball in his limited sample of 64.2 big-league innings last season. The right-hander has always gotten whiffs and the Brewers have proven they know what they're doing in regards to pitching. Chasing a full season's worth of starts would be a fool's errand, but the team clearly has high hopes for Woodruff in regards to both performance and workload.

Eovaldi threw a shutout in his second start of 2025 and pitched like a Cy Young candidate with a 1.73 ERA and 0.85 WHIP over 22 total starts for the Rangers before a rotator cuff strain ended his season in late August. The right-hander then underwent sports hernia surgery in October. While ostensibly healthy heading into 2026, Eovaldi should be considered a long shot to make 30 starts, something he's done only once over the last decade. Regression to his numbers seems inevitable, though tangible improvement can be found behind his success last season, as he dialed back his fastball usage in strategic fashion while trimming his walk rate back to elite territory. As he enters his age-36 season, the wheels are in danger of falling off, but Eovaldi is a legitimate ace when healthy.

Adames entered his first season with the Giants facing two uncertainties: how the move to Oracle Park would affect his bat, and whether his running game would hold up. The shift from hitter-friendly American Family Field to a park that suppresses offense showed up in his surface numbers, but not in his skills. His 108 wRC+ matched his final three years in Milwaukee, indicating his performance held steady after park adjustment, even if his 2025 wOBA dipped. His barrel and hard-hit rates ticked up slightly, while his strikeout rate reached a three-year high, keeping his batting average volatile despite power that plays anywhere. He attempted fewer steals, largely reflecting team philosophy. Overall, Adames continues to profile as a mid-tier shortstop.

Suarez's "HR or nothing" approach at the plate paid its biggest dividends in 2025, from his four-homer game in late April, to his season-ending career bests of 49 HR, 118 RBI, 40.9% fly ball and 47.6% hard-hit rates. Shifting his swing in that direction over the years has put him at an elevated risk of low batting averages, however, as well as peaks and valleys in his performance. That's not the kind of profile that seems likely to age well, and Suarez will play most of 2026 at 34 years of age. Expect some regression in the power department, though he should still put the ball over the fence frequently enough to remain a top-10 fantasy third baseman.

Bradish underwent Tommy John surgery with an internal brace in June 2024 but returned to start six games down the stretch. While command and control can lag after surgery, he showed little rust, striking out 47 batters against just 10 walks over 32 innings, with velocity in line with his healthy years. The performance was encouraging, but he has totaled only 104.2 innings across the majors and minors over the past two seasons. That likely points to workload management ahead, and expecting him to sustain last season's pace, even if it mirrors his healthy 2023, may be optimistic. A cautious approach is warranted.

Williams took a sizable, statistical step forward in 2025, shaving more than a run and three-quarters off his ERA while reaching the 30-start plateau for the first time as a professional, but his skill set remained a bit of a mixed bag. He had the majors' worst qualified walk rate (11.8%), the widest negative ERA-FIP differential (-1.33) and poor metrics in terms of contact quality allowed, signaling regression coming due. Still, Williams is only 26 years old, equipped with a 96.6-mph fastball and a pair of elite breaking pitches (curveball, sweeper) that make him especially tough against lefties, giving him growth potential that could neutralize those luck factors. It's probably best to treat his draft stock similarly to his 2025 fantasy finishes: SP24 (points), SP28 (rotisserie).

The Astros thought they had solved their problems at first base when they signed Walker to a three-year, $60 million contract in December of 2024, but he mostly ended up just being the club's latest headache. The veteran first baseman struggled out of the gate with a .210/.273/.357 slash line through the first two months of the season, and he was never quite able to dig out of that hole. Walker showed signs of life in July and August with an .831 OPS, but that type of production was the expectation for the full season, not just two months. He still launched 27 home runs -- his fourth straight year with at least 26 -- and had respectable RBI (88) and run (72) totals, but the lack of consistency was a major issue. Walker is a decent candidate to bounce back in 2026, with his power and run production providing a solid floor despite the fact he's coming off a disappointing season.

Gray and Lady Luck have been at odds for the last two years. In 2024, his ERA was pegged about a run too high by xFIP, and last season, his 4.28 ERA was deemed roughly a run higher than its estimators. His BABIP and HR/FB rate were elevated, while his LOB percentage was suppressed. Gray eclipsed 180 frames for the second straight season, which he had last accomplished in 2015. For the second consecutive season, his velocity slipped, but he waived his no-trade clause to join the Red Sox, who specialize in teaching pitchers to work off breaking balls and offspeed stuff, and Gray can throw multiple types. Gray's home runs have crept up over the past two seasons, and the Green Monster has a habit of turning routine flyballs into doubles, so Gray may need to get back in favor with Lady Luck. Father Time looms, but for now, Gray remains dependable.

No other active closer has more saves than Hader over the past five seasons. His 28.8 strikeout-minus-walk percentage lead all closers in that time, as well. Throw in the fourth-best WHIP and the second-best batting average against, and you may ask yourself why there is any reason Hader is not the first closer off the board in fantasy drafts. The answer to that question lies in the uncertainty surrounding his health, as he came down with shoulder soreness in early August and never returned to the mound, then dealt with biceps inflammation at the onset of spring training. It is also worth remembering that Hader was coming off a post-COVID high for workload from 2024 to 2025, which could help explain the injuries. Keep tabs on his progress as Opening Day approaches.

Nimmo put together another productive campaign in 2025, slugging 25 homers with 92 RBI, both career highs, to go along with 81 runs and 13 steals across 155 games with the Mets. Last season marked his fourth straight reaching 150 games, as Nimmo continues to distance himself from the injury issues that plagued him earlier in his career. In November, he was traded to the Rangers amidst rumors of a rift with former teammate Francisco Lindor, a move that looks like a wash for Nimmo in many respects. The outfielder gave up a bit in terms of OBP and was more aggressive in recent years as he took on more of a run-producer role, but he has the plate skills to transition back to leadoff duty if Texas prefers to go that route.

Altuve posted a 113 wRC+, his lowest mark in a full season since 2013. While his home-run output climbed to its highest level since 2022, his batting average dipped to a career low outside of the abbreviated 2020 season. A decade ago, that might have been written off as variance, but entering his age-36 season, it may instead point toward the early stages of decline. If that is the case, erosion can accelerate quickly, introducing more risk into a profile that has been remarkably stable for years. Altuve compensated for a modest drop in barrel rate by pulling more flyballs, though there is no guarantee that adjustment sticks. With age, the downside scenarios begin to outweigh the upside, but that reality is typically reflected in the draft cost, and his dual eligibility at second base and outfield still provides some appeal.

The Cardinals moved Contreras from catcher to first base last offseason, but the defensive move didn't bring significant change at the plate as he posted a .257/.344/.447 slash line with 20 home runs, 80 RBI and 70 runs in 135 games. A .791 OPS ended up being his worst mark since 2021, and that was largely fueled by his 8.2 percent walk rate, which was nearly five points worse than his 2024 mark. Being traded from the rebuilding Cardinals to the Red Sox in December should provide Contreras with the potential for more run production in 2026, especially since Fenway Park is more hitter friendly to right-handed bats than Busch Stadium. Contreras has a pretty well established floor with an average of 20 home runs, 59 RBI, 60 runs and a .252 batting average across the past five seasons, so he's a fairly safe mid-tier fantasy target.

Although a back issue cost him the first month-plus of 2025, Suarez swiftly recaptured his prior form as one of the game's best command artists, as for the fifth consecutive season he placed in at least the 70th percentile in terms of average exit velocity and hard-hit rate allowed. In fact, he tied for the season's longest consecutive quality start streak (10, May 10-June 29). These things appealed to the Red Sox, who, despite an overstuffed rotation, brought him on as a reliable, middle-of-the-staff innings eater. Fantasy managers should regard him the same way, understanding that such pitchers typically carry a little more value in points than rotisserie leagues.

Aranda's counting stats from 2025 don't really stand out on the surface as he finished with 14 homers, 59 RBI and 56 runs, but he remarkably did most of that damage before the end of July when a collision with Giancarlo Stanton sidelined him for nearly two full months. Overall for the year, he delivered a .316/.393/.489 slash line in 106 games, priming him for a full breakout if he can stay healthy in 2026. Aranda's batted-ball metrics ranked among the best in the league, so there shouldn't be much worry about that elite performance being luck driven. He also returned for three games at the end of the regular season and went 4-for-12 with two long balls, eliminating concern about injury carryover. Aranda should bat in the heart of Tampa Bay's batting order in 2026, and fantasy managers are likely going to have to invest heavily to nab him on draft day.

Imanaga is back with the Cubs for 2026 despite the team declining his three-year club option, since the club still tagged him with the qualifying offer, which ultimately led to the pitcher accepting it to re-prove his market viability next offseason. Imanaga had a hamstring injury in early May which kept him off the mound for six weeks. He made 20 starts before September and recorded eight wins with a 3.08 ERA, and 0.93 WHIP. However, his final five starts in September included a 6.51 ERA with velocity decline and 10 homers allowed in just 27.1 innings of work. Despite the decent overall numbers, his strikeout numbers dropped significantly to 7.3 K/9. The motivation is there for a great 2026, but are the skills?

Fairbanks remarkably avoided the injury bug in 2025 -- he had missed at least a month while on the IL in each of the previous four seasons -- and set personal bests with his 27 saves and 60 1/3 innings. While his raw stuff and underlying metrics, paled in comparison to his 2022-23 peak, he was plenty serviceable in the Rays' closer role. The Marlins, taking note of that and his 17 saves and 2.43 ERA away from homer-friendly George M. Steinbrenner Field, signed Fairbanks to handle their ninth inning, where he'll call a much more pitcher-friendly environment his home. Once the more durable, top-shelf relievers are off the board, this is a strong, risk/reward choice to fill out your pitching staff.

The Athletics traded Erceg to the Royals at the 2024 trade deadline, and after notching holds in his first five outings, he was installed as the closer. However, Kansas City signed Carlos Estevez in the offseason, relegating Erceg to setup duties last season. He delivered 23 holds and chipped in with a pair of saves and eight wins, but there was a noticeable change under the hood, as Erceg's strikeout rate plummeted nine points. His ERA was unaffected by the decline, as he posted a career-low mark, though estimators pegged it as more than a run too low. His velocity dropped a tick across the board, likely contributing to the strikeout dip. Erceg's season ended in mid-September with a shoulder impingement, but he's expected to be ready for camp. Monitor his velocity; without a rebound, he's risky as a reliable source of holds.

Dominguez has settled in as a whiff-generating, righty-dominating, short reliever -- and one who has been popular on the midseason trade market -- making him a good pickup for the bullpen-starved White Sox. His experience could prove useful in a prospective spring closer competition with Grant Taylor and Jordan Leasure, though Dominguez would still be helpful in holds leagues if the team prefers to go with a younger option.

Coming off a 6.14 ERA and an unremarkable spring, Palencia opened the season at Triple-A Iowa before being recalled in mid-April to add bullpen depth. He quickly impressed, posting a 1.20 ERA and 0.80 WHIP with 15 strikeouts across 15 innings, which earned him a save opportunity amid struggles from Ryan Pressly and an injury to Porter Hodge. Though he blew his first chance, Palencia converted his next five save opportunities and retained the job until a shoulder injury sidelined him in early September. He returned for the final week in lower-leverage work. With the Cubs adding quality setup options, Palencia has a clear path to build on last year's team-leading 23 saves. While his track record is lacking, a repeat performance could elevate him into a higher tier.

Albies had a season to forget in 2025 with a career-low .671 OPS across 157 games with Atlanta. Adding injury to insult, Albies suffered a hamate bone fracture in his left hand during the final week. He is expected to be fully recovered in time for spring training, but the second baseman's inconsistency in recent years makes him tough to trust entering 2026. Historically, Albies has done a disproportionate amount of his damage from the right side of the plate -- his struggles from the left side have led to calls for him to give up switch hitting. An All-Star as recently as 2023, Albies has shown little in recent years to justify enduring optimism, though at least the downward trends have not yet extended to his overall strikeout rate. Further, the 29-year-old still provides efficiency on the basepaths.

A 31-year-old journeyman, O'Brien added velocity to his sinker and spin to his slider and broke through for the 2025 Cardinals, ultimately earning himself their closer job in the month of September. That might give him a leg up in their spring competition for the role, and his ground ball leaning and ability to suppress hard contact does minimize the downside if he emerges. Monitor O'Brien's spring progress, which will ultimately decide whether holds or saves are his target, but there's enough opportunity here to make him a viable fantasy late-rounder.

Lodolo made huge strides in 2025, posting a 4.8% walk rate that ranked sixth among pitchers with at least 20 starts, while generating many swings-and-misses on pitches out of the zone -- he had the fourth-best chase rate among that same group -- before injuries largely interrupted his final two months. At the time, he had scored the 20th-most fantasy points among pitchers. Whether those injuries (a blister, an illness, a right groin issue) represent a recurring pattern is in question, but Lodolo could be on the verge of a full-season breakthrough with the adjustments he has made. He's a pitcher to watch during spring training, as he'd have a top-25 starter's ceiling with a standout March.

Shaky control and a knee injury sustained during a game of Hacky Sack ruined Uribe's 2024, which began with the promise of potential save chances (including in four of the team's first six games). He'd settle for a middle relief role to begin 2025, from which he was every bit as excellent as he was across the final three months of his 2023 debut campaign. Uribe led the league in holds (37) and was third among relievers in both ERA and hard-hit rate allowed. Plus, he managed six saves and a 1.89 ERA in 18 games between the regular season and postseason after stepping back into the closer role for an injured Trevor Megill. That breakthrough puts Uribe in direct competition with Megill for the team's ninth-inning role this season, with your league's inclusion of saves or holds ultimately determining Uribe's value. He'll be one of the best closers or holds-getters, however it shakes out.

A throwback type thanks to his elite-contact, batting average-but-minimal-pop hitting style, Arraez was a relative disappointment in 2025. He fell 12 points short of what would’ve been a fourth consecutive National League batting title, and the Padres struggled to find defensive positions at which to slot him due to his deficiencies in that regard. Teams might’ve seen similar issues with Arraez when considering him as a free-agent target, though the Giants ultimately saw enough in him to make him their everyday second baseman and probable No. 2 hitter. He’ll remain an underrated points league pick in that role, perhaps even from within the top 100 tier, while stabilizing roto teams’ batting averages.

At casual glance, Pepiot's 2025 has the guise of �spinning his wheels� or worse, a small step backwards. His ERA rose by more than a quarter of a run, he averaged 0.1 fewer fantasy points per start, and he whiffed only 24.6% of the hitters he faced after 26.3% the year before. Make no mistake, however, that the Rays' return to Tropicana Field for 2026 is a huge positive for Pepiot, who surrendered 17 homers (among 26 total) at what was the majors' seventh most-favorable home run environment in 2025. He's a capable, now built-up starting pitcher who could be ready to take another step forward into top-25 SP territory.

Kwan could not sustain the power gains from the prior season, though he still reached double-digit home runs for the second straight year. The 2024 spike was driven by more flyballs, and while he elevated the ball even more last season, the contact quality was not as strong, resulting in fewer homers and a career-low BABIP. Only three qualified hitters put the ball in play more often, keeping Kwan a steady batting average contributor, and he matched his career high with 21 steals. His durability also returned, as he missed just six games after appearing in only 122 the year before. Ignore the dip in power and draft Kwan for average and speed, with any home runs coming as a bonus.

"Well?! We're waiting!" It might feel like forever to fantasy managers, but it's important to remember that Holliday, the No. 1 pick of the 2022 Draft and consensus No. 1 prospect entering his 2024 MLB debut season, is still only 22 years old and just 427 professional games removed from high school. Not all prospects blossom immediately, and perhaps he's one of those who takes baby steps to get there. Holliday's metrics were so-so at best in his first full big-league campaign in 2025, but he did greatly improve his patience (95th percentile chase rate) and contact (80th percentile rate) during the season's second half, and he showed hints of future five-category rotisserie potential. That said, a fractured right hamate bone suffered in February will cost him important spring training time and likely land him on the IL to start the season. Holliday is still a high-upside middle-round pick, but picking him requires a bit of a leap of faith.

After hitting 232 home runs across a seven-year span (2018-24) in Japan, Okamoto suffered an elbow injury in a collision at first base, limiting him to a career-low 77 games. Ah, but what productive games they were! He hit .322/.411/.581 and made contact 87% of the time -- all of those career-best rates -- which bodes well for a smooth transition to the U.S. game. Okamoto figures to slide in at third base for the Blue Jays, where he'll benefit from hitting in the middle-to-lower portion of their deep lineup. As is the case with any Japanese hitter, his range of outcomes is wide due to the adjustment period required, but he's a well-rounded hitter who brings a lot of fantasy upside in the late rounds.

Now, where did that come from? Montgomery arrived in Chicago in early July and quickly went on an uncharacteristic power surge. Over a 37-game span a few weeks after his recall, he hit 18 home runs, matching his entire 2024 total across 130 minor-league games. And that's not to say that he can't do it again, as he had strong underlying hard-contact metrics, but his 17.2% HR/FB rate, which was eighth-highest in the league from his debut date forward, hints that there'll be some pullback. Montgomery might need to improve his plate approach in order to take another step forward in 2026. As it is, he's a late-round pick for mixed-league play.

Soler was limited to 82 games in 2025 due to back issues, which resulted in two trips to the injured list and cost him the final two months of the season. The veteran slugger wasn't particularly productive when available, finishing with 12 home runs, 34 RBI, 31 runs and a .215/.293/.387 slash line in 314 plate appearances. Soler is now entering his age-34 season, so the recurring back issues in 2025 could spell trouble moving forward, especially since he already wasn't the most consistent of hitters. Still, he's just two seasons removed from clubbing 36 homers for Miami, and he played in at least 137 games in both 2023 and 2024. Soler can't be fully written off despite the age and injury concerns.

Don't let the persistent trade rumors swirling around him dissuade you that Skubal is as good a choice to lead your fantasy pitching staff as anyone. He's coming off back-to-back Cy Youngs, and has made consistent, notable improvements in almost every statistical category across his six MLB seasons. Skubal set personal bests in ERA, WHIP, walk rate, K/BB rate, whiff rate and rate of hard contact allowed in 2025. Since July 1, 2023, he has a 2.37 ERA and MLB-leading totals in both wins (38) and strikeouts (571). He's also entering his contract year -- the very reason for said trade rumors -- which, while hardly a guarantee as a motivating factor, assures he'll play 2026 at full bore, and with a team that will provide him the necessary support to again thrive.

Bradley had an underwhelming 4.61 ERA in 21 starts for Tampa Bay in 2025 before being traded to Minnesota, where he struggled even more with a 6.61 ERA in six outings. He posted a career-worst 8.0 K/9 and 3.5 BB/9 last season but also had a career-best 1.2 HR/9. Bradley has shown flashes of brilliance since making his MLB debut in 2023 but has been mostly ineffective, with the drop in strikeouts negating the one area in which he still provided fantasy value. Bradley isn't guaranteed to begin 2026 with a spot in Minnesota's rotation, but the Twins seem likely to give him a chance to get back on track in the big leagues given how hard they committed to selling at the trade deadline last summer.

Baseball's top-scoring fantasy pitcher over the first four seasons of his Yankees career (2020-23), Cole missed the first three months of 2024 due to an elbow injury, then ultimately succumbed to 2025-ending Tommy John surgery last March. A 14-month recovery timetable would have him ready to rejoin the big-league club in May, though the variability of return date and initial performance level coming off that operation lends uncertainty to his 2026 draft stock. Cole will be one of the most important pitchers to track once he resumes game competition (exhibition or minor-league level) in the spring, but his skill set makes him one of the best IL stashes for prospective front-of-a-staff fantasy production in the season's second half (or even its final four months).

A ruptured quadriceps tendon prematurely ended what was an otherwise excellent year for Adam in setup relief, as he turned in a second straight year of a sub-2.00 ERA and at least 25 holds and 70 strikeouts in 2025. Keep tabs on his health once spring training opens. When healthy, he’ll almost assuredly serve as Mason Miller’s primary setup man and fantasy insurance policy. Adam’s skill set is top-20 caliber among relief pitchers, so expect a return to that form sometime before midseason at the latest.

Perez once again fended off Father Time as he continues to outproduce catchers more than 10 years his junior. Ignore his lowest batting average since 2018; his xBA was his best since 2020, and his xSLG was tops since 2021. His strikeout, barrel and hard-hit rates were all better than in recent seasons. His bat speed dropped a tick, but after all, it was his 14th season, much of that time spent squatting his burly 6-foot-3 frame behind home plate. The Royals are doing a good job keeping the veteran fresh by frequently rotating him through first base and designated hitter. The catcher position continues to be replenished with promising young talent, but last season's perceived slide and another year of mileage could depress the price enough to make betting on Perez remaining a top-10 backstop worthwhile.

After finishing seventh among pitchers in fantasy points over the final four months of 2024, Brown followed things up with six straight months of near-identical production (he'd finish sixth this time). A modest boost to his swinging-strike rate, while maintaining his elevated average fastball velocity, fueled a consistently excellent year, during which he never went more than three outings between quality starts. Brown appears to have leveled off, but he has done so as one of the premier talents at his position. He should be one of the first starting pitchers off your draft board in any format.

Just about everything that could possibly have gone wrong for Rutschman in 2025, his age-27 season, did. He hit just .203/.300/.332 across the first two months, made trips to the IL for both obliques (left in June, right in August) and was ultimately pressed for his job by top prospect Samuel Basallo. That competition is the biggest lingering issue, as both players appear likely to make the team in a catcher/DH combination for a team that has a lot of other DH alternatives. Rutschman was previously a budding points-league star thanks to his well-rounded offensive game and the promise of hefty DH time. With that no longer a guarantee, he needs a standout spring to rekindle a top-5 positional valuation in the format. That ceiling remains possible, considering his age and skill set, however.

Happ is entering the final year of his most recent contract, which is something to keep in mind for those who like factors such as contract years when targeting players. Happ has been a consistent on-base machine in recent seasons, but his batting average is now league average as the rest of the league has come down to his level. The switch hitter is at his best when facing righties as most of his homers come from the left side, but he has held his own hitting from the right side of the plate as well in recent years. His on-base abilities lock him in somewhere near the top of the Chicago lineup for 2026, but it will be a different batting order without the presence of Kyle Tucker, and the club's apparent reticence to spend big to replace him. Happ has been a 20/80/80/.240 producer for three straight years and expect a fourth.

After returning from Tommy John surgery in 2024, Springs was traded from the Rays to the A's last offseason. He went on to pitch a career-high 171 innings in 2025, reaching the 30-start threshold for the first time at 32 years old. The left-hander struggled early on last season, particularly in the first inning, leading the team to experiment with an opener in front of Springs a couple times. His performance improved after some adjustments, though his numbers started to slip again around the middle of August. Nevertheless, in the end, Springs led the A's in ERA, wins and strikeouts among other categories, making him the de facto ace of the pitching staff entering 2026. The swing-and-miss is way down at this stage of his career, but Springs will get a chance to build upon what he showed over the final three months with regular starts for an improving team.

Unable to maintain the elevated strikeout rate that earned him the Giants' closer role over the final two months of 2024, Walker was demoted back to middle relief after posting a 6.43 ERA over his first 16 appearances last season. He'd ultimately get another chance to close in August and September following the trade of Camilo Doval, but Walker's slider wasn't nearly as effective in 2025 as in the past, and he ultimately finished the season with MLB's fourth-most blown saves (7). Walker should begin 2026 as the team's primary ninth-inning option, with good enough command and a ground-ball leaning that would make him a useful mid-range fantasy option, but he'd need to make a significant adjustment in order to vault into the position's top 10.

Doyle broke out in 2024 with 23 homers, 30 steals and a .763 OPS during his second MLB campaign, but he regressed significantly last season with a .233/.274/.376 slash line in 138 contests. He still provided some power and speed production with 15 long balls and 18 stolen bases, but his run production was lacking with 57 RBI and 57 runs. He made strong contact at a similar clip to 2024 with a 44.6 hard-hit rate, which provides hope for a rebound in 2026 despite the down campaign. Doyle's elite defense in center field will help him to maintain a regular spot in the lineup, and his decent floor in homers and steals make him a bounce-back candidate with a solid floor despite a poor surrounding lineup.

Bibee fell ill with food poisoning and missed his Opening Day assignment, which set the tone for a queasy start to the 2025 season. He posted a 5.85 ERA through his first four outings for the Guardians, but the right-hander settled in and ultimately peaked at the right time with a 0.86 ERA and 0.71 WHIP over his final 21 regular-season innings to help Cleveland overtake Detroit for the AL Central crown. While Bibee does not possess an overpowering fastball, he has five secondary pitches, including a changeup that helps him neutralize lefty batters. His strikeout rate fell precipitously last season and lagged well behind the top-end arms in MLB. His home-run rate is also trending in the wrong direction, but Bibee limits walks and has pitched especially well at home at Progressive Field in his three seasons in the big-league rotation.

A submarining, ground ball-generating, righty-dominating short reliever, Rogers is one of the very best at his craft. However, you need to recognize the craft -- that of a locked-in, primary setup man rather than a flamethrower -- for what it is. He's a holds machine, owning 18% of the total number of 30-hold seasons across the past five seasons (he has four), with some of the most projectable ratios around. That's a nice thing to have in formats that reward setup men.

Sheehan's return from May 2024 Tommy John surgery couldn't have gone much more smoothly, especially since he returned to big-league action in only 13 months. From July 6 forward, he scored 185 fantasy points, 17th among pitchers, while posting encouraging 30.6% strikeout and 7.6% walk rates that represented a definite step forward from his 2023 numbers. Sheehan was considered one of the better pitching prospects before the injury, so he should take another step forward, particularly in terms of volume, in 2026. The Dodgers might keep him on an innings cap, with 130-140 being a good guess, but that's plenty for him to warrant mid-round consideration in fantasy leagues.

Burleson cut his chase rate down and saw immediate results in 2025, slashing .290/.343/.459 across 139 games with the Cardinals to win the Silver Slugger at the utility spot. He improved against lefties and led the team in OPS on the strength of improved patience and selectivity, though he ended up falling short of his 2024 totals in home runs, runs, RBI and steals due to missing time in the second half with a wrist injury. With Willson Contreras now in Boston, Burleson will take over as the everyday first baseman in St. Louis after splitting time between the outfield (74 games), first base (50 games) and DH (22 games) last season. The profile does not look out of place in the middle of a major-league lineup, and entering his age-27 campaign, Burleson still appears capable of more.

Winn's 2025 was going quite well until some knee discomfort in June revealed a slight tear in his meniscus which first required an injection and eventually led to him shutting his season down in mid-September to get a head start on the planned arthroscopic surgery. Winn had six homers heading into June but hit just three more the rest of the season, yet he was still able to steal seven bases in eight attempts on the bum knee. The injury helps explain away a lot of the traditional statistical decline Winn experienced in 2025 and gives reason to think he could be in store for improvement in 2026 assuming better luck on the health front. He may not get to 20 homers, but 20 steals with his speed and some increased opportunities on base is certainly possible. This is an underrated four-category contributor whose down 2025 offers a 2026 discount.

Volpe played through a partially torn labrum in his left shoulder for much of 2025 and underwent surgery in October, which is expected to sideline him for the start of 2026. The young shortstop provided fantasy managers with solid counting stats (19 home runs, 18 steals, 72 RBI and 65 runs in 153 games), but his .212/.272/.391 slash line left a lot to be desired. Playing through the injury obviously affected Volpe's offensive performance, but it's unclear exactly how much it influenced the actual results given that his .663 OPS was nearly identical to his first two big-league campaigns. He still has 20-20 upside and appears locked in as the Yankees' primary shortstop for another year, but a delayed start to 2026 and inconsistency make Volpe a volatile fantasy target.

One of baseball's best bat handlers -- he's one of four players with at least 85% contact and 27.5% line-drive rates and 500 plate appearances over the last two seasons combined -- Donovan's skill set makes him one of the most underrated points-league players, even if he's only a back-of-your-roster utility type in rotisserie formats. Traded to the Mariners in February, he’ll likely serve as their leadoff man against right-handed pitchers, giving him more of a matchup lean in shallow mixed leagues but also boosting his run-scoring potential on the whole. Donovan's ceiling isn't especially high, but he's likely to deliver another top-100 fantasy point total in 2026.

O’Hearn has carved out a “strong side of a straight platoon” role over the past three seasons, batting .280/.346/.445 against righties in that time, which makes him one of the more useful late-round picks in fantasy leagues that allow daily transactions. His move to Pittsburgh, and pitcher-friendly PNC Park, does lower his prospective number of actionable matchups somewhat, but he’s someone to keep in mind as you round out your roster.

Bogaerts has been on a rather bizarre run in recent years with almost impossibly low counting stats for an established player of his caliber. A four-time All-Star and twice a 100-RBI bat during his time with the Red Sox, he has not reached even 60 RBI in a season with the Padres. Bogaerts missed time in 2024 with a fractured left shoulder and has now settled at exactly 11 homers in consecutive seasons. After transitioning to second base in 2024, Bogaerts moved back to shortstop in 2025, and with that he loses the dual eligibility that boosted his fantasy utility. The age-related decline began earlier for Bogaerts than most, but at 33 he is still a plus player for San Diego and the stolen bases help his case for continued mid-round interest.

Torres enjoyed a resurgent campaign in his first season with Detroit, making his first All-Star team since 2019, though he regressed hard in the second half with a .659 OPS compared to an .812 OPS before the break. After the Tigers were eliminated from the postseason, Torres underwent sports hernia surgery. He was cleared for full activity in December. Despite the late slide, the Tigers extended him the qualifying offer for 2026, which Torres accepted. With that, the 29-year-old will return to second base and presumably to the top third of the order after batting almost exclusively first or second under manager A.J. Hinch last season. While Torres does not pack the power or speed to be especially exciting for fantasy purposes, he does enough to be worthwhile in most formats.

Castillo has outpitched his peripherals since joining the Mariners in 2022, and it may be by design rather than just good fortune. With the Reds, Castillo was an extreme groundball pitcher which helped offset the homer-friendly Great American Ball Park. In the Pacific Northwest, he is leaning more on his four-seam fastball, which generates more flyballs. T-Mobile Park suppresses home runs, so while his home-run rate has risen, it remains reasonable, and the added flyballs are driving a BABIP between .267 and .285 over the past four seasons. The change in approach has sent his strikeout rate into freefall, denting his fantasy allure and increasing his dependence on a low BABIP, a slippery slope. Entering his age-33 season, Castillo's floor is more wobbly than usual, and without strikeouts, the ceiling is limited.

For what seemed like the umpteenth year in a row, Snell was excellent when available to his fantasy managers � which didn't happen especially often. Among the 61 pitchers who have made at least 87 starts over the last four seasons, he ranks first in strikeout rate (31.9%), second in ERA (2.76), fifth in fantasy points per start (13.9) and seventh in hard-hit rate allowed (34.8%). The problem? That's exactly the number of starts Snell made in that time, which is under 22 per year. It's remarkable that he has been able to maintain such a high level of productivity around his many absences, but credit the Dodgers for being among the best at maximizing pitcher workloads and utility when available. We see no reason for that to change now. So, how lucky do you feel?

Stott put together a respectable if unspectacular campaign as the Phillies' regular second baseman in 2025, hitting 13 home runs and stealing 24 bags across 147 regular-season games. He sat occasionally against left-handed pitching and did little against southpaws when given the opportunity with a .575 OPS and one homer in 123 PA without the platoon edge. A plus on defense, Stott figures to remain Trea Turner's double-play partner in Philadelphia for the foreseeable future despite his shortcomings. Citizens Bank Park is hitter friendly and Stott isn't asked to carry much of the load offensively, for better or worse. Manager Rob Thomson experimented with Stott in the leadoff spot last season but eventually settled on him being a lower-third bat even against right-handed pitching.

Diaz's wRC+ declined for the second straight season despite a gain in power. Over the prior two years, his batting average closely tracked his xBA, but last season he finished 16 points below expected, driven largely by an unusually low line-drive BABIP. He also posted a career-low hard-hit rate, working against batting average. Added loft did push his barrel rate to a career high, and he paired that with the lowest strikeout rate of his career. Diaz grades as a below-average defender, so reversing the offensive slide will be important if he is to remain among the most heavily used backstops after his 567 plate appearances ranked sixth among catcher-eligible players last season. More line drives falling in would help, but he also needs to hit the ball with more authority and with greater selectivity.

One of the few things that went right for the disappointing 2025 Orioles, Laureano performed as he had in his early days in Oakland for four months, then maintained that level of production following a midseason trade to the Padres, before a fractured finger ended his year in the final week. With his boosted power metrics and balanced platoon splits, he earned a place as the Padres' starting left fielder and heart-of-the-order hitter, the latter boosting his RBI potential. Everything in Laureano's 2025 metrics supports his ability to repeat the effort, making him a solid late-rounder for fantasy play.

Dingler took over as Detroit's primary backstop in 2025 and delivered a quality rookie campaign, finishing the regular season with 13 homers, 57 RBI, 54 runs and a .278/.327/.425 slash line in 126 games. Previous No. 1 catcher Jake Rogers is coming off a second straight disappointing season at the plate, so he's likely to stick in the backup job to begin 2026. Dingler didn't walk much with just 23 free passes but had a 23.5 percent strikeout rate. Dingler also provided strong defensive value behind the plate, which will be key to maintaining playing time at a premium defensive position, though he may not quite be ready to truly play every day like the top catchers in baseball. Repeating a strong average with 10-15 homers and modest counting stats is a fair expectation in 2026.

Elder's 5.30 ERA and 1.39 WHIP over 28 starts in 2025 are ugly on the surface, though his 2.82 ERA and 0.99 WHIP across his final seven starts provide some reason for optimism heading into 2026.  He cut down on the walks (2.9 BB/9) but also struck out fewer batters (7.5 K/9) compared to 2024. Atlanta will be looking to return to contention after a down year, and the right-hander may need to carry that late-season form into spring training in order to have a chance of making the Opening Day rotation. Regardless, Elder is likely to make some starts for Atlanta at some point in 2026, but his days could be numbered if he struggles early on.

After a three-year run as the Yankees' closer and seven years in MLB as a reliever, Holmes signed with the Mets as a starter in December of 2024 and held his own last season in his first year as a full-time starter. The right-hander had his workload managed down the stretch but finished 2025 with a 3.53 ERA, 1.30 WHIP and 129:66 K:BB across 165.2 innings (33 appearances). His move to the rotation predictably resulted in reduction in velocity and strikeouts, but Holmes was able to mostly offset that by being one of the most prolific groundball starters in baseball (55.9 percent groundball rate). A 7.0 K/9 certainly lowers Holmes' upside, but he'll still have a fair amount of fantasy value if he can replicate his run prevention from 2025.

Wacha is coming off a season in which he threw the most innings he has worked since his 181.1 frames way back in 2015. Wacha has avoided the injured list the past two seasons and continues to provide consistent if boring production to fantasy managers with safe ratios and a below-average strikeout rate. Wacha has a deep repertoire of pitches built around his changeup, and he will throw all six pitches to both righties and lefties, using his abilities to keep hitters off balance to make up for what he lacks in velocity. This approach is a perfect fit for pitching in Kansas City where Wacha has allowed just 13 home runs since joining the club compared to 19 in his road starts. This season should be yet another consistently steady campaign for the veteran, but you will need to find your strikeouts from other pitchers.

Mize hit the injured list in May with a hamstring strain but still made his first All-Star team in 2025, going 9-3 with a 3.15 ERA and 1.22 WHIP over 88.2 innings with Detroit in the first half. He slumped to a 4.92 ERA and 1.34 WHIP after the break, mirroring the team's collective slide. The right-hander shaved his walk rate to just 5.7 percent while upping his strikeout rate to a career-high 22.2 percent last season, though he got touched up with the long ball on occasion, with the splitter in particular yielding a surprising number of homers. After being drafted No. 1 overall in 2018, Mize underwent Tommy John surgery in 2022, missing the entire 2023 season as a result. No ace but from a bust, Mize has re-emerged in recent years as a capable mid-rotation arm for the Tigers.

Coming off what was a top-10 fantasy starter's 2024, Miller's follow-up campaign was effectively ruined by bone spurs in his elbow, the ailment sending him to the IL twice and nearly doubling his ERA. Though his fastball velocity and whiff rate on his splitter improved over the season's final six weeks, his ERA over that time was nevertheless 5.62 and he couldn't find consistency at any point all year. Miller did avoid offseason surgery, but only spring training can demonstrate whether the winter's rest has helped him. He still has that ace-caliber stuff when healthy, so a strong spring would make him a potentially profitable late-round pick.

After four straight seasons of above-average production, Reynolds slipped to slightly below the norm, driven by a spike in his strikeout rate and a BABIP that didn't align with his batted-ball mix. He failed to gain the typical batting average boost that comes with more groundballs and line drives. His batting average dropped 30 points from the prior season, while his slugging finished 45 points below 2024. That said, his xBA was actually one point higher, and his xSLG was only 25 points short of the previous year. The downturn extended to the running game, as Reynolds went just 3-for-5 in steal attempts after going a combined 22-for-25 over the prior two seasons. Just 31 years old, Reynolds appears capable of a rebound if his strikeout and flyball rates move back toward earlier levels.

An elbow issue that required offseason surgery bumped Herrera off catcher and to DH around midseason, at a point in 2025 too early for him to log the requisite time to maintain eligibility behind the plate. It's a shame, as his skill set -- solid contact, plate discipline skills and pop, as well as aggressiveness on the bases -- is intriguing for fantasy purposes from a catcher, but much more commonplace from a DH (a position that lets you use anyone). The Cardinals claim that Herrera should be able to return to catching duties in 2026, but his defensive limitations there might slow that process. Considering he'd have a top-10 ceiling at catcher, take a flier on him late and keep your fingers crossed.

Paredes' 2025 season can best be summed up by what could have been. The third baseman hit 20 homers in 102 games while being forced to miss two full months with an acute hamstring tear that initially looked like a season-ending injury. Paredes' extreme pull and flyball approach are an ideal fit for his home stadium, yet just 11 of his 20 home runs came at Daikin Park. Paredes previously hit 31 homers around the challenges of Tropicana Field and the changing of the dimensions in Baltimore in 2023, so we know what a full season of his approach is capable of, but that same approach also leaves him quite susceptible to batting average risk, because his batted balls that do not leave the yard are either cans of corn or routine groundball outs to the left side due to his slow foot speed. He might hit 40 home runs in 2026, but he may also struggle to hit .240.

After years of outperforming his expected ERA, Gallen didn't get much favor from Lady Luck in 2025. He had the eighth-widest ERA-xERA differential among qualifiers, he posted a career-worst 21.5% strikeout rate and he had an ERA over 4.00 in five out of six months. Still, Gallen continued to pitch effectively enough deep into games, his 33 starts being second-most and 192 innings eighth-most in the league. Plus, he had a 3.32 ERA over his final 11 starts. Back with the Diamondbacks after a long winter on the free-agent market, Gallen is a strong points-league option as one of the more durable starters out there.

Caglianone had one of the more disappointing rookie seasons in 2025, posting the worst batting average (.157) and OPS (.532) among those with at least 200 plate appearances, while sporting one of the league's worst chase rates. But, to be fair, he was also only a little over a year removed from being a two-way player at Florida, with only 95 games of minor-league experience focusing on hitting alone at the time. Caglianone did flash gaudy bat speed and Barrel metrics, and the 20 homers he hit in 66 minor-league games underscore his massive potential in that department. The Royals' decision to shrink the outfield dimensions at Kauffman Stadium should also help him. If Caglianone is swinging well in Cactus League play, make sure to scoop him up late in the hopes he's ready to break through at age 23.

Fantasy managers love Castro’s positional flexibility, and now they’ll love another thing about him: He’ll call Coors Field his home. Besides his defensive utility, Castro’s most marketable skill is his speed, but he’s capable enough with the bat to capitalize upon the favorable hitting environment. He’s an ideal round-out-your-roster type, able to be mixed and matched for his Coors games and against weaker starting pitchers. Just don’t expect any miracles when he’s playing on the road.

Heading into the 2025 season, Semien had been a model of reliability playing in the fifth-most games since he came into the league in 2015 while playing in three organizations with solid-to-spectacular production from his middle-infield positions. However, age appeared to catch up with him in 2025 as he had the worst season of his career at the plate which was eventually ended by a foot injury resulting from a foul ball. The Rangers, reticent to spend on the free-agent market, decided to trade Semien to the Mets for Brandon Nimmo, which could be a boon for a fully healthy Semien. He should now find himself nestled between Francisco Lindor and Juan Soto at the top of the Mets lineup providing him both ample RBI chances as well as plenty of run-scoring opportunities. He deserves one more chance from fantasy managers.

The Phillies have talked about wanting to utilize Marsh as an everyday outfielder rather than a platoon player since acquiring him in 2022, but his continued struggles against left-handed pitching (.577 OPS in 2025) have essentially made that impossible. The good news is that he continues to crush righties and posted a .300/.356/.482 slash line against them last season. His production on the basepaths dropped significantly with just seven steals after he posted a career-high 19 in 2024, and 11 home runs marked his lowest total since 2022 while his 43 RBI and 59 runs were also underwhelming. Marsh's ratios continue to be strong, but the lack of volume significantly caps his counting stats and limits his upside in most formats.

Senga was as unhittable as any pitcher in baseball through the first third of the season. He won seven of his first 13 starts with a 1.47 ERA and 1.11 WHIP, striking out 24 percent of the batters he faced. An acute hamstring injury sent him to the injured list in mid-June, and that is when the fun ended. Senga came back for nine games after the injury, won none of them, and pitched to a 5.90 ERA and 1.69 WHIP while seeing his K-BB drop to an unsightly eight percent. Senga was eventually sent to Triple-A Syracuse and was not much better there. Senga's forkball is still amazing, but he had to use his non-forkballs too frequently to get back into counts. The Mets will hope an offseason of rest allows Senga to rediscover his early-2025 ways quickly in 2026.

Grisham had an improbable 2025 season which saw him double his previous career high of 17 home runs, hitting 34 for the Yankees in his final year before free agency. He was one of the early advocates for the torpedo bat style, but that alone did not fuel this breakout power season as much as Grisham's overall deliberate approach to hitting. He is very patient at the plate and went hunting for fastballs early in counts, and often found them with 21 of his 34 homers coming from fastballs. Before you give Yankee Stadium's short porch too much credit, understand Grisham's home OPS was 200 points lower than it was on the road and he hit just 13 of his 34 home runs at Yankee Stadium last season. Grisham took the qualifying offer to firm up his free agency vitae with the thought Yankee Stadium cannot possibly punish him two consecutive seasons.

McKinstry is a sneaky late-round pick in deeper mixed leagues, particularly those that use roto scoring, thanks to his positional flexibility -- he qualifies at three different spots -- and stolen base contributions. He has swiped at least 16 bases in each of the last three seasons and had 46 extra-base hits in 2025, while registering personal bests in most offensive categories. McKinstry’s contact quality remains only mediocre, however, and his statistical profile lacks much in the way of matchups he can exploit. Regard him as a back-of-your-roster type, but not a player likely to make many advances in 2026.

Smith was one of the stories of spring training last year when his long-shot bid to make Houston's Opening Day roster was successful, but the harsh realities of Major League Baseball eventually set in. The third-baseman-turned-outfielder hit the skids in the summer months and finished with a .154/.247/.242 line in the second half. GM Dana Brown acknowledged after the 2025 season that Smith could require more time back on the farm, pointing to the need for greater consistency. It wasn't all bad as Smith had his moments, including a two-homer game in April, but the way his rookie year ended suggests a reset may be necessary. The upside is still there long term for the 2024 first-round pick whom the Astros acquired from the Cubs as part of the return for Kyle Tucker.

Seemingly blocked at his primary position at the MLB  level by Adley Rutschman, Basallo parlayed .270/.377/.589 rates and 23 homers in 76 games for Triple-A Norfolk into his first opportunity with the Orioles once Rutschman's oblique issues resurfaced in mid-August. Basallo would struggle through a too-aggressive approach at the plate, batting only .165 while striking out over 25% of the time, but he flashed decent pop and was a plenty serviceable backstop. He's expected to serve in a catcher/DH partnership with Rutschman in 2026, from which both will hinder the other's playing time somewhat, but also from which both could be fantasy-relevant and even prospective top-10 positional values. The long-term sky's the limit with this kid.

Clement ended up being a key contributor for the Blue Jays throughout 2025, batting .277 with 35 doubles, 50 RBI and 83 runs in 157 games. He hit just nine home runs and stole six bags, both of which were drops from 2024 when he recorded 12 apiece. He makes a ton of contact and had low strikeout and walk rates (10.4 percent and 4.7 percent, respectively). Clement played in at least 29 games at third base, second base and shortstop while also making 15 appearances at first, which is more playing time than a utility player usually gets. Clement doesn't really profile as a true lineup regular, and he could be pushed out of a starting role, depending who else the Blue Jays sign this winter. He can have some deep-league appeal due to the high average, run potential and defensive versatility but likely won't get enough volume to be a reliable fantasy contributor.

Apparently, the fastball velocity drop he experienced in his final year in Japan was no mirage, as Sasaki struggled early in that regard in his first taste of the U.S. game, posting a 4.72 ERA and 15.6% strikeout and 14.3% walk rates in eight starts before a shoulder issue cost him the next three months. He'd return with elevated velocity and filthy stuff out of the bullpen in September and the playoffs, even handling some save chances in October, which offered a glimpse of his elite potential. Sasaki should be stretched out again to start this spring and, if he's looking similarly good -- monitor that velocity, which needs to be closer to 98 than 96 mph -- he'd be a breakout candidate, albeit one who might face an innings cap.

Manzardo exhausted his rookie eligibility with 156 plate appearances in 2024, but he got in his first full MLB campaign last season and produced 27 home runs, 70 RBI, 47 runs and a .234/.313/.455 slash line in 142 games. He did most of his damage against right-handed pitching with a .789 OPS, though he still slugged .419 versus lefties. Manzardo doesn't offer much defensively but still made 56 appearances at first base, so he'll have eligibility there rather than solely as a designated hitter. He should be a steady presence in Cleveland's lineup in 2026 but may not have true everyday volume given his struggles against southpaws, though his power potential could help him see more chances than a standard platoon player.

Throughout 2025, Steer was held back by some upper-back issues which never put on him on the injured list but did hamper his ability to drive the ball with authority on a consistent basis. Steer once again hit 20-plus homers for a third consecutive season, and he was pacing to set a new career high if not limited by the nagging injury. He lost nearly 90 plate appearances from the previous two seasons both due to injury and the club giving Sal Stewart some extra time at first base down the stretch. It was surprising to see Steer's stolen-base production fall off as much as it did in 2025 with Terry Francona's lead foot taking over the running game, but that too could easily return if Steer is 100 percent healthy for 2026. The 2023 season was a great one for him with an .820 OPS, but Steer has yet to replicate that level of production.

Jung was limited to just 46 games in 2024 due to a wrist injury, but he was able to stay mostly healthy last season and played in a career-high 131 contests. Unfortunately for fantasy managers, his offensive production still took a hit, and he finished 2025 with a .251 average, 14 homers and a career-low .390 slugging percentage. The Rangers demoted Jung to the minors for a few weeks over the summer, and he did fare a bit better the rest of the way with a .732 OPS, but he was still far from a consistent contributor. The power potential is obvious given the 23 homers that Jung launched as a rookie in 2023, but injuries and inconsistency have made him a volatile fantasy option with a seemingly low floor.

One of the unluckiest pitchers of 2025, with a league-high .362 BABIP, and the second widest ERA-FIP differential in the wrong direction, among qualified relievers, Jax could be one of the position's biggest sleepers with some correction in those departments. Combine his past two seasons and he has the third best K/BB ratio (5.49), fourth-best FIP (2.21), and 62 saves plus holds (18th among relievers), underscoring his elite skill set. As spring training dawns, the Rays don't have a clear closer, a role from which Jax could be a top-10 positional fantasy option if they shift off their longstanding tendency to �mix and match� out of the bullpen. He'll be a top source of holds or saves nevertheless, making him one of the top relievers to target once the clear, elite closers are off the board.

Teel, the primary piece in the December 2024 Garrett Crochet trade, brought his intriguing combination of plate discipline, pop and smarts on the basepaths to the south side of Chicago beginning last June, putting forth one of the better beneath-the-radar campaigns among rookies. Among those with at least 250 plate appearances, his .375 OBP ranked third and his .349 wOBA sixth. From his debut date forward, he had the 12th-most fantasy points among catcher-eligibles of any experience level (140). Teel figures to again rotate with fellow youngster Edgar Quero between catcher and DH, though it's important to note that he's the more integral piece in the team's future plans. Teel could be ready for a big step forward in 2026, making him a catcher with upside to target if you're going the cheap route at the position.

Estevez is coming off a fantastic season for Kansas City which saw him lead all of baseball with 42 saves for an 82-win club. Any concerns the talented Lucas Erceg would steal saves were quickly set aside as Estevez refused to give up any ground in the bullpen. He does not have the big strikeout rates of other closers in the game, but over the past two seasons, Estevez has the third-lowest ERA of all active closers and does not get himself into trouble with walks or homers. The fact Kansas City plays in a high rate of late and close games due to an inconsistent offense only helps Estevez get the ball on a regular basis. Estevez is not the sexiest closer, but he gets the job done and he should one again save 30-plus contests in 2026.

An adjustment to his batting stance fueled a semi-breakthrough for Barger, who hit .291/.342/.568 with 14 home runs across a 60-game stretch early in the year and reflected significant boosts in Barrel and hard-hit metrics for the full season. He'd cool off later in the year, batting .205/.270/.360 with six homers over his final 49 regular-season games, before putting forth strong showings in the ALCS and World Series. Barger's skill set is not without its limitations, as he's a weak defender and struggles against lefties, making him both a platoon and late-inning removal risk. Still, he's capable enough in the power departments to warrant a late-round pick in larger mixed fantasy leagues.

Tovar was hampered by injuries for much of the first half of 2025 and ended up playing in just 94 games on the year, finishing with nine home runs, five steals, 33 RBI, 44 runs and a .253/.294/.400 slash line. That line was a bit worse across the board compared to 2024, with slugging percentage being the major drop since his homer total was nearly cut in third. Despite some inconsistency, Tovar posted career bests in strikeout and walk rates (25.1 percent and 5.5 percent, respectively). The Coors Field effect has definitely been in play with a home average of .339 compared to .172 on the road. Tovar has showcased a decent floor for a mid-tier shortstop and should be able to get back around 20 long balls and double-digit steals with a healthy campaign in 2026.

After moving to a full-time starting role in 2023, Lugo survived with modest strikeout rates by limiting walks and suppressing home runs, helped by pitcher-friendly parks in Petco Park and Kauffman Stadium. He reached last season's break with a 2.67 ERA and 1.08 WHIP, seemingly following the same script, but a 4.17 xFIP hinted at looming issues. Elevated walk and home-run rates were hidden by an 87.9 percent left-on-base mark, and the correction came quickly. Over his final seven starts, Lugo posted an 8.35 ERA and 2.01 WHIP as his command and control unraveled, potentially tied to a back injury that ended his season early. On top of the strikeouts being a weak point, the late-season breakdown leaves added questions going forward.

Weathers didn't make his season debut in 2025 until mid-May due to a forearm strain, and he landed back on the injured not long thereafter due to a lat injury. The left-hander finished the campaign with just eight starts, though he pitched well in those appearances with a 3.99 ERA, 1.28 WHIP and 37:12 K:BB over 38.1 innings. Weathers hasn't made more than 16 appearances in a season since working as a swingman as a rookie with the Padres in 2021. He has a 3.75 ERA and 1.21 WHIP across the past two seasons, but he simply hasn't been healthy enough to move the needle for fantasy managers. Weathers could factor into the Yankees' rotation for as long as he can take the mound, but he's likely to have a limited workload even if healthy given that he's yet to throw 100 frames in a season as a big leaguer.

McLain has had two seasons of productive counting-category volume with the Reds, but it came around him missing the entirety of the 2024 season, and the long layoff was evident. McLain took a lot of time to round into form in 2025, as he was hitting just .178/.273/.300 heading into June with more steals (11) than extra-base hits (10) in just over 200 plate appearances. He righted the ship from there on out with a more respectable .242/.314/.367 line with 23 extra-base hits and another seven steals. The final numbers were decent for a middle infielder hitting toward the bottom of the lineup, but the 70-point dropoff in batting average was tough to carry. The rust should all be gone now and McLain projects to resume his worthwhile counting production with a boost in batting average somewhere in between his 2023 and 2025 figures.

Westburg's output closely matched the prior season, though injuries again played a central role. A broken hand limited him to 107 games in 2024 and wiped out much of the second half, while last year brought a late-April hamstring injury sidelining him for almost six weeks, followed by a mid-August ankle sprain that cost him another month. The skill gains he showed before the 2024 injury didn't carry over, and his plate discipline has slipped from his minor-league days, with a walk rate just under five percent across the past two seasons. Improved health and greater patience could allow more of his power to surface. He isn't an aggressive base stealer by nature, and the injuries further reduced his running. Limited to 85 games, Westburg also came up three games shy of second-base eligibility in most formats.

Durbin gave Milwaukee and its fans an exciting immediate return on investment from trading Devin Williams in the offseason. Durbin leveraged a successful showing in the Arizona Fall League to earn a mid-April promotion to Milwaukee and never looked back. Durbin had the fifth-lowest strikeout rate for all batters with at least 500 plate appearances in 2025 and was a pest at the bottom of the Milwaukee lineup as a tough out at the plate while also being tough on the bases, stealing 18 bases in 24 attempts. Durbin will be hard pressed to hit more homers in 2026, but there is certainly room for batting average growth with better batted-ball fortunes and stolen bases with the accompanying improvement to his on-base percentage. The skills are there for a .280 average and 30-plus steals with better luck. Following his trade to the Red Sox, he'll likely start at third base.

Baty failed to make an impact after making the Mets' Opening Day roster last year and was demoted to Triple-A in late April, but he was called back up a couple weeks later and was able to get on track from there. The third baseman played in 130 games and posted a .254/.313/.435 slash line with 18 home runs, eight steals, 50 RBI and 53 runs. The club's roster upheaval during the offseason should give him a clear path to starting nearly every day in 2026, and he has clear 20-10 potential coming off the mini-breakout, though there's certainly some risk given he's yet to establish year-to-year consistency. Baty finished 2025 on the IL due to an oblique issue, but that shouldn't affect his availability for the start of 2026.

Few active players have followed a smoother career aging curve than Realmuto, who at 34 years old last season saw predictable dips in his power and bat-speed metrics, but not nearly enough to dissuade the Phillies from bringing him back on a three-year, $45 million deal. They recognize his worth on the defensive side (important in fantasy because of how it props up his playing time), as well as his above-average skills with the bat as well as on the basepaths. Realmuto is no longer the fantasy star behind the plate that he was, but he was a top-15 player at the position in both roto and points leagues last year. That’s a threshold he can certainly reach again in 2026.

Alvarez has had an interesting past 12-18 months. The catcher suffered a hamate bone fracture in early March which delayed the start to his 2025 season, and then he was demoted to Triple-A after a slow .236/.319/.333 start which included struggles behind the plate. He returned with a vengeance just after the break and hit .276/.360/.561, reminding everyone of his potential even while playing through a sprained UCL in his right thumb. That UCL injury means he has needed surgery to repair the UCLs in both of his hands as well as the hamate bone fracture in the past year. His offseason preparation may once again be affected, but those second-half numbers remind us of the tremendous upside in this young man. The balance between risk and reward is the big question.

Kelly got off to a scorching start last season, batting .361/.500/.820 with eight home runs through the Cubs’ first 36 games, before regression grabbed hold and restored him to borderline top-25 fantasy catcher status. It’s not that that’s without value, but he’s more of a high-floor than high-ceiling type, best known for his keen eye at the plate rather than his pop. Kelly should again work in a partnership behind the plate for the Cubs, getting enough at-bats and hitting enough homers to be the kind of pick you want as your mixed-league No. 2 catcher (if your league requires one).

A handy swingman who was productive for the Rangers in both roles in 2025 (2.72 ERA in eight starts, 2.93 in 25 relief appearances), Latz figures to compete for a rotation spot this spring. It's the role from which he'd be more fantasy-relevant, even if only from a matchups perspective. His mediocre walk rate and penchant for fly balls puts him at heightened risk of bad outings, which would be a bigger deal if those outings are shorter. Should Latz emerge in the Rangers rotation, consider him in the late rounds as you're filling out your staff.

A season that began with optimism after Vientos' 2024 power breakout ended in frustration, though some of it was unwarranted. His wOBA dropped by more than 50 points, but his xwOBA fell only 14 points. Some of the previous season's enthusiasm was aided by good luck, and that swung the other way last season.
