Vientos struck out less and hit the ball harder, but he didn't receive the same favorable results. His barrel and hard-hit rates remain well above average, but even with last season's improvement in contact, he still strikes out at a well above-average clip, and with just two career steals in four seasons, he needs power to be productive. Even if partly undeserved, Vientos' struggles last season, especially down the stretch, have his 2026 role in jeopardy. Marcus Semien is slated for second base, pushing Brett Baty back to third. Vientos could slide to first base, but Jorge Polanco was signed and is the likely fit there.

Correa should be projected for zero steals, with his last one coming in 2019. He began last season with the Twins but was dealt back to Houston at the trade deadline after producing a .267/.319/.386 line over 95 games. Feeling rejuvenated, Correa improved to .290/.355/.430 over 51 games with the Astros. The only differences in his approach were a bit more patience and more flyballs, perhaps due to seeing the inviting and familiar Crawford Boxes. Correa hit seven homers in four months with the Twins, and then clubbed six in two months back with the Astros. New this season is dual eligibility at third base and shortstop, which will be useful since he profiles as a corner or middle infielder in mixed leagues. The upside is minimal but the added flexibility helps his appeal.

In his 11th MLB season and with team No. 8, Armstrong set personal bests in games (71), innings (74), WHIP (0.81), BAA (.157), saves (9) and holds (12), thanks mostly to much better performance with his secondary pitches. He returned to his first big-league organization (Cleveland) during the offseason, where he'll serve as a setup man in the Guardians' well-stocked bullpen. Armstrong should be a reliable source of holds and ERA for fantasy teams in that role.

Abreu joined the Triple-Digit Club for the third straight season, reaching 100 strikeouts yet again, with only Cade Smith and Mason Miller achieving the milestone twice over that span. Abreu spent most of the season setting up Josh Hader, recording 25 holds, but he was pressed into closing in mid-August and delivered seven saves in eight chances. Curiously, he posted a 4.24 ERA and 1.53 WHIP during that stretch, but it was fueled by an uncharacteristically high .442 BABIP, over 60 points higher than the mark he posted the previous two seasons. It is not clear if Hader will be ready to start the season, which will drive up Abreu's price. Abreu sits atop the list of closers-in-waiting with the ability to protect ratios while contributing to strikeouts.

Wells had a productive sophomore campaign for the Yankees despite some concerning trends in some of his performance indicators. Wells increased his aggressiveness at the plate, reducing his walk rate by nearly five full percentage points while his strikeout rate increased by over five percentage points. That resulted in his batting average falling further below the league average but still closer to an acceptable level for the catcher position. Wells still finished tied for fifth with 21 homers as a catcher and seventh with 71 RBI. Wells significantly improved his production against lefties, hitting six home runs while also batting .240 against southpaws. He also hit more homers on the road than at home, which goes against prevailing knowledge. His elite framing skills, as well as Ben Rice shifting to first base in 2026, should allow Wells to push for a career high in plate appearances this season.

Nelson made some changes to his approach in 2025, and the results followed. He remains a fastball-heavy pitcher, but against lefties he used breaking balls rather than changeups as his secondary offerings and greatly improved his results. Lefties had hit .267/.328/.482 off him the previous two seasons, but the new approach led to a .191/.25/.309 outcome in 2025. Nelson also found more success pitching at home, which had been a tremendous problem for him each of the previous two seasons. Nelson did not even join the Arizona rotation on a full-time basis until early June but went 5-2 with a 3.38 ERA and 1.10 WHIP over those 20 starts. Nelson looks primed to repeat his 2025 success with more innings as a full-time starter who has worked hard to reduce some overall weak spots in his game.

Leiter's adjustment to big-league competition has been slow, but appreciate his 2025 growth for what it was. He posted a 3.28 ERA, seven quality starts and a 26.3% strikeout rate across 13 second-half starts and lowered his walk rate to 7.0% over his final nine outings. Equipped with a high-90s fastball and maturing slider and changeup, Leiter could be ready to take a big step forward in 2026. He has the top prospect pedigree, making him one of the more potentially profitable prospective late-round picks for your draft.

A shoulder injury cost Yoshida half of 2025, though he’d finish on a high note, batting .354/.369/.494 in his final 23 regular-season and Wild Card Series games. While he figures to be Boston’s DH against right-handed pitching, keep their cluttered first base and outfield pictures in mind, as further missed time or any struggles could result in a dip in playing time. Yoshida is best used as a matchups option in daily formats, but he’s worth taking in the late rounds of deep mixed leagues.

Musgrove missed all of last season while rehabbing from the Tommy John surgery he underwent in October 2024, but he should be good to go for the start of 2026 given that he was throwing multi-inning bullpen sessions late last season. The veteran right-hander has a 3.25 ERA, 1.12 WHIP and 9.6 K/9 since the start of the 2020 campaign, but there are major question marks regarding his durability as he enters his age-33 season. Musgrove made just 36 starts across 2023 and 2024 due to injuries (even before the Tommy John injury), and he's now coming off a lost season and major elbow surgery. Regaining his strong form in the first year back wouldn't be unheard of, but Musgrove's additional injury issues add another layer to consider. His ceiling is that of a top-end starter, but the floor here is zero.

From a rates perspective, Diaz's 2025 was up there alongside any of his best statistical seasons, including his outrageous, 57-save 2018. The main drawback was his garnering only 31 save chances -- an inexplicably low total for a closer from an 83-win team. Diaz departed the Mets during the winter for a Dodgers team that has finished second in the majors in save chances in both of the last two seasons, despite their never truly having a singular ninth-inning choice over that time. While manager Dave Roberts could exploit a matchup every now and then, Diaz's contract and raw stuff almost assuredly will earn him the role for 2026, from which the right-hander is as good a bet to top his position in fantasy value as anyone.

For about one month of 2025, Yates looked like the top-shelf fantasy reliever he was in 2024, albeit exchanging saves for holds in L.A., but a hamstring injury in May threw derailed him and never afforded him the opportunity to get his season back on track. Despite this, the Angels signed him to compete, and perhaps serve as the favorite, for their closer role. So, who is the real Yates? The answer is probably something in-between his past two seasons, though it'll bring a lot of injury risk now that he's 39 years old. He's as risk/reward as prospective closers come.

Stanton didn't debut for the Yankees in 2025 until mid-June due to tendinitis in both elbows, but his presence was worth the wait as he posted 24 home runs and a .944 OPS, which was his best mark since his MVP campaign in 2017. He played in just 77 games but still provided plenty of run production with 66 RBI, though his actual runs total (36) was unsurprisingly much lower given his awful sprint speed. A 34.3 percent strikeout rate was the highest of Stanton's career, but he continues to hit the ball as hard as anyone in baseball. Expecting a repeat of that production over a larger sample wouldn't be wise, but Stanton has clubbed 24-plus homers each of the past five seasons and seems likely to do so again in 2026, even as he enters his age-36 season.

Sheets was non-tendered by the White Sox in November of 2024 and eventually landed with the Padres on a minor-league deal in February, but he ended up being one of the better success stories of 2025. He posted an .833 OPS with 11 homers in his first 51 games of the season, and although he cooled off down the stretch, he still finished the campaign with 19 home runs, 71 RBI and a .252/.317/.429 slash line in 145 contests. There's certainly a question of sustainability given the .680 OPS he posted during his four years in Chicago, but Sheets' batted-ball metrics indicate the improved results were well deserved. While his volume may be capped a bit since he's expected to continue working as a strong-side platoon player, Sheets could push for 20 homers in 2026.

Kikuchi found another gear after being traded to the Astros at the 2024 deadline, largely by shaving half a tick off his curve and changeup, which made his fastball play up. That showing led the Angels to sign him to a long-term deal, banking on some carryover. Instead, all of his pitches lost velocity last season, whether by design or age-related decline. The reduced velocity aided his offspeed and breaking pitches but hurt his four-seamer, contributing to his lowest strikeout rate since 2019 and his highest walk rate in three years. At 35 years old, and with 97 starts over the past three seasons, Kikuchi faces a number of questions including whether the velocity returns. The left-hander can still contribute, but his best use comes at home in favorable matchups.

Bader stayed healthy for long enough last season to play in a career-high 146 games, showcasing elite defense while stealing double-digit bases for the fourth consecutive year. He also put forth the best underlying power metrics he has in nine seasons in the majors. Bader’s rising strikeout rate, however, makes him increasingly a batting average risk, and the move to San Francisco lands him in one of the game’s worst power environments. Fantasy managers should value Bader closer to his three-year average than 2025 alone, as he’ll contribute in the primary roto categories, but without much in the way of upside.

Brought in to help patch up a Milwaukee rotation that was hit hard by injuries early on, Priester ended up playing a prominent role in the Brewers' 2025 success after struggling to find his footing between Pittsburgh and Boston to begin his career. The right-hander totaled 13 wins against three losses during the regular season for the best W-L percentage in all of baseball (.813). He was especially good during a 16-game stretch in the middle of the season in which he went 10-2 with a 2.74 ERA and 1.04 WHIP over 91 innings. A below-average strikeout rate should temper enthusiasm, but Priester keeps the ball on the ground and the Brewers have earned the benefit of the doubt when it comes to pitching. Perhaps an appeal to authority, this pick nonetheless makes sense in the later rounds.

Back-to-back big years in Korea, at the ages of 27 and 28, put Song firmly on the MLB radar, and the Padres saw his defensive utility as a boon to their offense. He managed a 25/25 season overseas in 2025, and he has a good chance at breaking camp as the Padres’ second baseman, if not a rotating starter all over their infield. Monitor Song’s progress in adapting to MLB pitching during spring training, as he’d be a late-round sleeper if he looks ready to play every day.

Bassitt keeps on keeping on as one of the game's more durable innings-eaters, totaling the 17th-most fantasy points among starting pitchers over the past four seasons, despite a No. 39 average annual finish in that department during that same time span. That's the benefit of locked-in, 30-start types in points leagues, especially those who possess Bassitt's combination of above-average control and ability to suppress fly balls and hard contact. He's an ideal guy to draft late and stream, especially against weaker teams, as he has an ERA nearly a run lower in his career against losing (3.19) than .500-plus (4.11) teams.

After eight mediocre seasons between Philadelphia and Boston, Pivetta broke out in his first year with San Diego in 2025, going 13-5 with a 2.87 ERA and 0.99 WHIP across a career-high 181.2 innings during the regular season. Not only had Pivetta never posted an ERA under 3.00 prior to last year, he hadn't posted a mark under 4.00. A flyball pitcher, Pivetta has often struggled with homers, but he cut his home-run rate way down and was especially stingy with the long ball at home in Petco Park. Although he hadn't enjoyed a high level of success prior to 2025, Pivetta often tantalized with his strikeout rates. The late bloomer will continue to take the ball every fifth day for the Padres, and expectations should be heightened but realistic.

Handed the Brewers' closer role at the onset of last season following the trade of Devin Williams, Megill upped both his fastball velocity and strikeout rate to score the eighth-most fantasy points among relief pitchers through late August, when he was lost for a month due to a flexor strain. Megill would return in time for the Brewers' playoff run, although Abner Uribe's performance in the interim thrusts the position into somewhat of a spring competition entering 2026. Megill figures to be the favorite to close, with similar top-10 positional production after his back-to-back elite campaigns, though this is a situation to watch throughout March.

King made huge strides with both his control and command of what would otherwise be a lackluster fastball-sweeper combo last season, posting a 2.78 ERA and MLB’s ninth-most holds (27). Though he struggled to keep the ball in the yard (10 HR), he’s generally good enough at minimizing hard contact that he should improve in that department in 2026. Consider him a top source of holds, with fantasy-worthy ratios.

Schwellenbach was well on his way towards earning Cy Young votes when a small fracture in his right elbow brought his 2025 to an abrupt stop in June. Between the final three months of 2024 and the first three of last season, he scored the fifth-most fantasy points among pitchers (502), thanks in part to a high-90s fastball and an elite, whiff-generating splitter. Unfortunately, Schwellenbach's elbow issues persisted through the winter, and he required Feb. 18 surgery to remove loose bodies from his elbow. The Braves placed him on the 60-day IL at the onset of spring training, so he'll miss at least the first two months of 2026 and perhaps more than that. Schwellenbach has the upside to be a top-20 option at his position when healthy, but he's as risky a pick as they come if you're aiming to stash him for the second half.

The Tigers opened the season without a defined closer, and Vest was not part of the early mix. After posting a 1.17 ERA and 0.52 WHIP with nine strikeouts in 7.2 innings, however, he earned the first of what became a team-leading 23 saves. Manager A.J. Hinch leaned most heavily on Vest while still playing matchups, which allowed him to add four holds. Illustrating reliever ERA volatility, Vest logged his highest ERA since 2022, even as his xFIP and SIERA were their lowest over that span. He is not as overpowering as the top-tier closers, but he fanned more than a batter per inning over the past three seasons. Detroit bolstered their bullpen with fellow right-handers Kenley Jansen and Kyle Finnegan, yet Hinch remains noncommittal on roles. Vest fits well in leagues that count holds, as he should continue to work in high-leverage spots regardless.

Peterson is a 6-foot-6 lefty who gets good extension on his sinker, which allows him to keep the ball on the ground. He made a career-high 30 starts for the Mets in 2025, pitching to a 4.22 ERA and 1.37 WHIP over 168.2 innings. After throwing his first career shutout in June, Peterson was named to his first All-Star team, but his season went in the wrong direction from there. His final five starts were particularly ugly, with Peterson allowing 26 earned runs in 18.2 frames to skew the overall numbers. The groundball rate and advantageous home park can only do so much for a pitcher with marginal swing-and-miss, especially when the walk rate is a tad high. At 30 years old, he should continue to enjoy stretches of success when things are breaking right, but history says they will be fleeting.

After years of Camden Yards inflating his power numbers -- he has hit 64 of his 103 career homers there -- Mullins' mediocre metrics in that department were exposed following his midseason trade to the Mets. He hit just .182/.284/.281 in 42 games for the Mets, and those park translations carry some worry now that he'll play for the Tropicana Field-housed Rays. Mullins remains a good enough defender with 30-steal speed to remain a solid roto late-rounder, but his points-league value has taken a hit in his new digs.

Injuries again marred Moreno's season, as he appeared in fewer than 100 games for the second straight year. He was batting .270/.324/.414 in mid-June when he was finally placed on the IL after being hit in the hand two weeks earlier. The fractured finger sidelined him for more than two months, and after returning he posted an impressive .311/.397/.466 line over 30 games. For the season, he set new personal bests in barrel and hard-hit rate while hitting more flyballs to drive power. That came at the cost of a higher strikeout rate, though it remained well below average. Moreno's typically strong defense graded as league average, but he played fewer games behind the plate, especially down the stretch when he often served as the DH. It's unclear how much of last season's gains will carry over, and durability remains a concern.

Among 2025’s most unexpected outcomes was Baez’s first-half rebound, earning him an All-Star nod. The accolades came after three straight disappointing seasons to begin his six-year, $140 million contract with the Tigers, culminating in a 2024 that was one of the league’s worst by any player. A .337 BABIP through June made it clear last year’s hot start was almost entirely fluky, and he regressed to .219/.225/.315 rates and a 29.0% strikeout rate thereafter. It paints the picture of a highly risky fantasy pick, albeit one who might see enough time and contribute just enough power and speed to warrant a late-round roto selection.

A year after playing 153 games, Cowser was limited to just 92 due to a fractured thumb, a rib issue and a concussion. He broke his thumb sliding into first base on Opening Day weekend and missed just over two months. He collided with an outfield wall in early August and missed over a week due to a concussion. Earlier in the season, he also ran into an outfield wall and hurt his ribs without an IL stint. After the season, it was revealed he fractured two ribs, which may explain his .197/.273/.384 line for the rest of the season, though his production was even worse in the prior nine games, five of which came after returning from his thumb injury. A rising strikeout rate drove last season's decline. With 14 steals in 14 attempts, Cowser offers five-category upside, but the strikeouts create a shaky floor.

Lux's first year with the Reds didn't look all that different from his time with the Dodgers after he was traded in January. He played in a career-high 140 games and had a .269/.350/.374 slash line, with his five home runs being half the total he posted in 2024. He also tallied 53 RBI and 49 runs scored while doing most of his damage against right-handed pitching (.761 OPS vs. RHP and .466 OPS vs. LHP). Lux's 11.2 percent walk rate gives him some lineup stability, but the lack of counting stats limits his fantasy upside. He split most of his playing time between left field and designated hitter, with just 17 appearances at second base removing his eligibility there in most leagues. Lux is a high-floor, low-ceiling player that is likely to be limited to a strong-side platoon unless he can reverse his career-long struggles versus southpaws.

Sanchez was in the midst of a typical season for the Marlins in 2025 with 10 homers, nine steals and a .256/.320/.420 slash line through 86 games, but he was traded to the Astros at the summer deadline and never got on track with his new team, batting .199 and finishing with a .611 OPS in 48 games for Houston. Sanchez's production prior to the trade was pretty close to the .750 OPS he posted the two previous seasons, so it's reasonable to expect him to rebound to that level in 2026, especially given the small sample with the Astros. He isn't likely to see much action versus left-handed pitching but should see enough volume to be fantasy relevant as a strong-side platoon player, assuming he beats out Nathan Lukes for the left field job in Toronto. Sanchez doesn't have a ton of upside but is a decent target to round out a fantasy outfield.

Santander was one of the biggest signings of last winter as he landed a five-year, $92.5 million contract with the Blue Jays, but his first campaign in Toronto was a disaster with a .175/.271/.294 slash line and just six homers, and his second will see him on the injured list for most of the year following February left labral surgery. Once he heals, Santander will have every opportunity to get back on track for Toronto given what remains of his contract, and the surrounding lineup should offer plenty of opportunities for counting stats.

Scott got off to a hot start in 2025 with a .290/.357/.403 slash line, two homers, 11 steals, 18 RBI and 20 runs in his first 37 games, but he struggled to a .529 OPS in 101 contests the rest of the season. He still provided single-category fantasy value with a total of 34 stolen bases, but his .296 slugging percentage was the worst in baseball among players with at least 450 plate appearances. Scott's strong defense in center field should help him to retain a regular role in the outfield for the rebuilding Cardinals, but the organization could look to see what else it has if he doesn't make some improvements at the plate.

Lowe showcased his potential during his first full MLB season in 2023 with 20 homers, 32 steals and an .835 OPS, but the past two years have been marred by injury and poor production. The outfielder had two more IL stints in 2025 due to oblique issues and was limited to 108 games. He struggled at the plate when available, posting a .220/.283/.366 slash line, though he still provided fantasy managers with a bit of power and speed with 11 home runs and 18 stolen bases. Lowe's main upside at this point is steals as he has 79 in 403 career games. He is simply unplayable against lefties (.459 OPS in 2025), so his volume is going to be capped by a platoon even if he can stay healthy. Lowe can provide fantasy managers some value if everything is going right, but the past two seasons have showcased how low his floor can be, and he may not have much longer of a leash with the Rays.

Berrios has logged the third-most innings since over the past five seasons, trailing only Logan Webb and Kevin Gausman, and it may have finally caught up with him. Berrios' season ended with right elbow inflammation which kept him off the postseason roster and potentially out of the 2026 Jays rotation. The club signed both Dylan Cease and Cody Ponce in the offseason, and it has said the latter was added as a starter. That currently leaves Berrios on the outside looking in unless Trey Yesavage falls into the same missteps Bowden Francis did this past season. Berrios' skills have slowly been eroding but it would be surprising to see him left out of the rotation all season as the club defends its AL pennant. The uncertainty around the status of his right arm may keep Berrios just cheap enough on draft day to turn him into an endgame value for 2026.

February surgery derailed Horwitz’s chances at being a fantasy sleeper last spring and, upon his return in mid-May, he put up near-identical numbers to those from his encouraging 2024. While he has a great plate approach -- a handy skill for points-based fantasy play -- his contact-quality metrics are average at best. That’s a problem for a player who calls an extreme pitchers’ park his home. Horwitz, no longer a second baseman after just one appearance there in 2025, is a corner infielder for deeper mixed leagues.

The Angels called Schanuel up a little over a month after drafting him with the 11th overall pick in 2023, and he has been learning on the job in the years since. Not your prototypical slugger at first base, Schanuel's offensive game is built around patience, putting the ball in play and striking out at a low clip. He has totaled just 25 homers over the past two seasons even with everyday at-bats, but Schanuel was batting a healthy .274 last season before a HBP in July knocked him off course. Eventually, he landed on the IL with a bone bruise in his left wrist. The experience he has gained against big-league arms should serve him well, but Schanuel still seems to have the same limitations entering his age-24 campaign. An increase in flyball rate helped a bit with his ISO and SLG last season.

Burger was acquired by the Rangers last winter and was coming off back-to-back seasons with at least 29 home runs, but he struggled early in 2025 and missed time due to oblique, quad and wrist injuries. The slugger never fully got on track and closed out the campaign with 16 homers and a .236/.269/.419 slash line in 103 games. He walked at just a 3.3 percent clip, earning only 12 free passes in 376 plate appearances. Burger still made strong contact with a 48.5 percent hard-hit rate, so there's some hope for a power resurgence in 2026 if he can stay healthy. Burger should have a pretty regular role for the Rangers, splitting his playing time between first base and designated hitter.

Numerous factors have worked against Lawlar getting an extended chance in Arizona, from Eugenio Suarez’s handling third base in 2024, to Lawlar’s thumb surgery last spring, to his own need to find another defensive position. A onetime top-10 overall prospect, Lawlar will experiment in the outfield in the hopes the Diamondbacks can jump start his career. He hit .313/.403/.564 with 11 homers and 20 steals in 63 games for Triple-A Reno last season, and he’s still only 23 years old, so don’t forget about him as a prospective breakthrough candidate if he’s looking good during Cactus League play.

The No. 2 overall pick in the 2023 Draft and a top-10 overall prospect entering his 2025 rookie season, Crews put forth solid power (7 HR) and speed (11 SB) numbers across his first 45 games, though his free-swinging nature (27.7 K%) led to a miserable, .196 batting average. An oblique strain would then cost him nearly three months, after which point he delivered more of the same, but with the same 50%-plus ground ball rate that must improve for him to truly realize his full power potential. Crews should get a long look for a starting role during spring training and, as he matures, he'll at least provide a solid stolen bases total for roto managers. He's more of a profitable late-rounder there than in points leagues, though he still has a high long-term ceiling for any fantasy format.

Jenkins, the Twins' first-round pick in 2023 and one of baseball's top-rated prospects each year since, has dealt with his share of injuries thus far as a pro, but his .295/.399/.464 line through 192 career minor-league games underscore his massive offensive potential when healthy. Assuming better luck in the injury department, he should be ready to break into the rebuilding Twins outfield before midseason. Jenkins' skill set should play well in points leagues, and he's a potential five-category player for roto formats as well. Be sure to add him the moment he's promoted.

Jeffers traded power for average last season -- 12 homers for 40 points in BA, specifically. He improved his chase rate in 2025 and started to take off in the second half (.297) before a concussion sidelined him for a stretch in September. The backstop returned during the final week, gaining a clean bill of health heading into the offseason. It would be nice if he could now add power back to the profile, but regardless of how the stats have been distributed, at the end of the day Jeffers' bat has been above league average three years running. While the team context is a slight drawback, he projects to retain the lion's share of the workload in Minnesota, which gives him an edge over other second-catcher options.

First, the good: On a per-start basis, Greene's skills took a noticeable step forward in 2025, as he set personal bests with his 31.4% strikeout and 6.2% walk rates, 68.8% rate of first-pitch strikes and 99.5 mph average fastball velocity. Then, the bad: He spent more than a month on the IL for the fourth consecutive season, this time missing 85 days across two stints for a groin strain. It underscores Greene's risk/reward status for fantasy leagues, as his raw stuff makes him a legitimate Cy Young contender when he's healthy --which he unfortunately hasn't been fully across any of his four MLB seasons. Considering every pitcher seems to be an injury risk these days, however, and that Greene will play 2026 at a prime-age 26, reward seems to be the smarter driving draft-day force.

It's becoming more common for players selected during the Rule 5 Draft to stick around with their new club, but it's not often that they end up being one of their new team's best players. That was the case for Smith, whom the White Sox selected from the Brewers during the 2024 Rule 5 Draft. The right-hander posted a 3.81 ERA, 1.20 WHIP and 145:58 K:BB across 146.1 innings during 2025, leading the Chicago rotation in most major categories. He limited the long ball pretty well with a 1.0 HR/9 but gave up a lot of hard contact, so there is some risk of regression, especially given the underwhelming defense behind him. Still, Smith has upside and could take a step forward in year two, and he should have plenty of volume on the rebuilding White Sox in 2026.

Control issues and an extreme fly ball-lean caused Uceta's 2025 to get off to a slow start, as he had a 5.53 ERA during the season's first half. Things improved from there, however, as he posted a 1.78 ERA and 35.5% strikeout rate in his 29 second-half appearances, re-establishing himself as one of the league's better setup relievers. With Pete Fairbanks no longer in Tampa Bay, Uceta could get a look in the ninth inning, whether full-time or as part of a committee arrangement. His skill set is likely to lead to game-over-game inconsistency, but the sum product should be that of a top-30 fantasy reliever.

Norby's trial run in Miami after being acquired at the 2024 trade deadline went well with a .760 OPS, but his first full season with the club in 2025 was less productive with a .251/.300/.389 slash line. He was limited to 88 games due to oblique, wrist and quad injuries, and he clubbed just eight home runs while recording eight stolen bases, 34 RBI and 42 runs. He improved his strikeout rate to 26.7 percent, and it's possible the injuries played a role in his power drop. Norby should be able to provide double-digit homers and steals if he can stay on the field in 2026, but any production beyond that isn't guaranteed and may not come with strong ratios.

Narvaez was acquired from the Yankees in a rare trade between longtime AL East rivals and opened the season as Connor Wong's backup, but Wong's early injury and subsequent struggles allowed Narvaez to seize the regular catching job. He delivered a modest 97 wRC+ yet still batted cleanup for a month during a strong second-half run. His barrel and hard-hit rates sit slightly above average, though his aggressive chase tendencies create too much swing-and-miss and cap his offensive output. Narvaez is slated to be the primary catcher this season, and while Wong held that role a year ago before regressing, Narvaez offers a stronger skill set and is the superior defender, even finishing as a Gold Glove finalist. He profiles as a cost-effective No. 2 catcher in mixed leagues.

Granted a starting role for the first time over the final three-plus months of last season -- he started 74 of the White Sox’s final 82 games between 1B, 2B and DH -- Sosa exploded for 18 home runs and 58 RBI. That RBI total was the most among 2B-eligible players over that time. Unfortunately, it came with some of the worst plate discipline in baseball, and an HR/FB rate more than 2% greater than the league average, making him a top regression candidate. Sosa’s skill set can be handy for filling out a roto lineup, but he’d need more patience to be a similar contributor in points leagues.

With Mason Miller now in San Diego, opportunities abound at the back of the Athletics bullpen. Sterner, who thrived late with a 1.40 ERA, 34.0% strikeout rate and seven holds over the final two months of 2025, should capture a late-round role, from which he'll add many holds and/or saves to the mix. An extreme fly ball lean (34.1% rate), coupled with the team's hitter-friendly home environment in Sutter Health Park, does put him at some risk for blow-ups, but he's a potential sleeper among late-round relievers.

Thanks to improved fastball velocity and the return of his whiff-generating slider, Speier emerged as a late-inning force for the AL West champion Mariners in 2025. His 24 holds ranked 16th in the league, and sixth among lefties. Plus, he lowered his walk rate to a sparkling 4.5%, fifth-best among qualified relievers. Speier returns as one of the team's primary setup men, from which he should again fill fantasy teams' holds and K's categories.

Wallner received his longest look in the majors in 2025 and clubbed 22 home runs in 104 games, but his numbers were otherwise pretty underwhelming with a .202 average, 40 RBI and 47 runs. His 29.1 percent strikeout rate was actually a major improvement from 2024, and he also had a strong 12 percent walk rate. The swing-and-miss in his stroke is obvious, but Wallner consistently makes strong contact when he connects and has a good eye at the plate. He actually fared better versus left-handed pitching than right (.790 OPS vs. .771 OPS), so he may be able to avoid a platoon. Wallner may not end up providing fantasy managers with much production outside of home runs, but the upside is there for him to do more, and the opportunities should be there on the rebuilding Twins.

Ashby adapted brilliantly to a multi-inning reliever role in 2025, his blend of elite ground ball, strikeout and hard-hit rates giving him a strong base of raw skills. It's a profile that should make him one of the better relief wins/holds/matchups-driven saves combo types, though the Brewers do have a decision to make on him this spring: Does he remain in that role, or would he provide them more utility out of the rotation? Keep tabs on Ashby's spring usage, as he could be a matchups-oriented starter with some upside if stretched out for the role.

Thanks in large part to greater reliance upon, and performance from, his curveball, Leahy cut 128 points off his OPS split against lefties in what was ultimately a breakthrough 2025. The Cardinals, seeing this, are giving him a long look as a starter this spring, with the adjustment elevating his fantasy potential (particularly on the matchups front). Leahy's upside might not be great, but if he's throwing well and emerges in the rotation in March, he'd warrant deep-mixed or NL-only consideration.

O'Hoppe hit 19 home runs while operating as the Angels' primary catcher in 2025, but he batted just .213 and provided horrible run production with 43 RBI and 35 runs. His strikeout and walk rates (30.8 percent and 5.4 percent, respectively) also left a lot to be desired, and the underwhelming production resulted in veteran Travis d'Arnaud taking on a larger role than initially expected. O'Hoppe's batted-ball data was still strong however, so there's reason to believe he can get back on track in 2026. That being said, he would seem to have a limited ceiling since his power is modest, and he isn't likely to stand out in batting average or run production.

Dominguez had a serviceable, yet far from Mickey-Mantle-esque, rookie season, though his modest second-half production (.236/.300/.318 rates) and defensive shortcomings caused the Yankees to ease off him in left field both in September and during the postseason. He's still only 23 years old and with decent power potential -- his Statcast hard-hit rate placed in the 85th percentile -- but to this point of his career, his most bankable fantasy asset is his speed. Dominguez might be ready to take another step forward in his second full season, but without a standout March, he's more of a late-round sleeper in roto leagues rather than in points formats.

Nootbaar played in a career-high 135 games in 2025, but his fantasy production dropped despite the increased volume since his .686 OPS was nearly 90 points worse than his career mark entering the season. Even though he had 80 more plate appearances than any other season, he saw his counting stats remain the about same, finishing with 13 home runs, 48 RBI and 68 runs while slugging just .361. However, Nootbaar still ranked near the top of the league in hard-hit rate (50 percent) and average exit velocity (91.3 mph), which puts him in a strong position to rebound in 2026. He underwent surgery on both heels in October and isn't guaranteed to be fully recovered by Opening Day, so his rehab progress is worth monitoring.

Gimenez was traded from the Guardians to the Blue Jays last winter, but he continued on his downward trajectory and finished the 2025 regular season with a .210/.285/.313 slash line in 101 games. He totaled seven home runs, 12 stolen bases, 35 RBI and 39 runs, with the steals production being especially notable coming off two consecutive 30-theft campaigns. Two month-long stints on the injured list due to quadriceps and ankle injuries may have played a role in that reduction. It's worth noting that his sprint speed did drop almost a full tick to 28 mph. Regardless, Gimenez doesn't offer broad fantasy appeal, though he could be a viable single-category contributor with a rebound on the basepaths, which wouldn't be a major surprise in his age-27 campaign. His elite defense should help to keep him in the lineup even if the offensive struggles persist.

Lee got his first full season in the majors in 2025, and much like the Twins as a team, it was largely a disappointing campaign. He played in 139 games and clubbed 16 homers with three steals, 64 RBI and 50 runs while posting an underwhelming .236/.285/.370 slash line. He split playing time between shortstop, second base and third base and will have eligibility at all three positions in 2026, but he's expected to work primarily at shortstop following the departure of Carlos Correa to Houston. Lee often hit for a high average in the minors but otherwise didn't stand out much statistically. He doesn't offer much speed and likely doesn't have much power upside beyond what he's already shown, so his fantasy ceiling is fairly limited, though he should get plenty of volume on the rebuilding Twins.

Crawford posted a career-worst .202/.304/.321 slash line across 105 games in 2024, but he bounced back last season with a .265/.352/.370 line in 157 contests. He set a career high with eight stolen bases and also posted the second-highest homer total of his career (12). The run production was limited with 58 RBI and 69 runs, which is a bit disappointing given that he spent half the season batting leadoff, though he did spend the other half hitting eighth or ninth. Crawford's plate discipline remains one of his best skills at the plate, and he had an 11.5 percent walk rate and 18.7 percent strikeout rate in 2025. The production last season was pretty close to Crawford's career averages, so it's a decent barometer for his expectations in 2026.

Murphy hasn't quite been the elite catcher Atlanta was expecting when it traded for him and signed him to a six-year extension in December of 2022, as he delivered a second straight season of underwhelming numbers in 2025. The veteran backstop played in just 94 games and missed the final weeks of the season to undergo surgery for a right hip labral tear, but the emergence of Drake Baldwin played a bigger role in his reduced playing time throughout the season. Murphy launched 16 home runs, but he batted below .200 for a second straight year and had a career-worst 31.2 percent strikeout rate. It's possible the hip surgery he underwent could help him to get back on track since he had been playing through the injury for years, but he appears likely to miss at least the first month of the season. At this point a best-case scenario likely would be Murphy serving in a timeshare at catcher with Baldwin once healthy, with their respective 2025 performances pointing toward Baldwin as the lead horse.

Stephenson bounced back in 2024 with 19 homers and a .782 OPS in 138 games, but he got off to a rocky start last season as an oblique injury delayed his debut until May. He then missed time during the second half due to a fractured thumb, and he wasn't quite as productive when available with a .231/.316/.421 slash line in 88 contests. Stephenson still provided quality power and run production with 13 home runs, 50 RBI and 40 runs, but a 33.9 percent strikeout rate was a career worst by a significant margin. Stephenson should be able to get back to 2024 levels if he can stay healthy, though he likely won't be relied upon as a true everyday catcher given his injury history. He has every incentive to put it all together in 2026, which is his final year of arbitration eligibility.

Emerson is the type of prospect who is very good at many things yet lacks eye-popping skills or stats in any one department. He hit .285/.383/.458 with 16 homers and 14 steals in 130 games across three minor-league levels in the Mariners system in 2025, all while playing solid shortstop. With a strong spring showing, Emerson could either break camp with the team or earn himself an early-season promotion, though his 20 years of age say he might need some time to get fully acclimated to MLB pitching. Nevertheless, he's a top dynasty prospect and a surefire add in all redraft leagues once he does arrive.

McNeil will change coasts in 2026 following a December trade from the Mets to the A's. In the years since winning the batting title in 2022, McNeil has fallen well short of those same heights, and in fact has sunk to .241 over his last 934 PA. He ended his time in Queens with just six home runs at home over his final two regular seasons, compared to a combined 21 on the road in that span. Despite Citi Field suppressing his power, McNeil at least reached a double-digit homer total each of the last three years. The thump is generally lacking, but he added to his walk rate in 2025 and the move to Sacramento in 2026 provides a park boost while solidifying playing time at second base. Entering his age-34 season, McNeil carries dual eligibility (2B/OF) but is not much of a contributor on the basepaths.

After years of trade rumors, the Rockies finally dealt McMahon at the summer deadline in 2025, sending him to the Yankees. His production remained largely the same in 2025, though his .214 average was a career worst, while he did club 20 home runs for a sixth straight full season. Despite the decent power numbers, he continues to showcase limited upside for run production with 53 RBI and 62 runs. However, landing in the Bronx certainly raises that ceiling even with him likely to hit toward the bottom of the lineup. McMahon's defense at third base brings the Yankees defensive stability, so he should receive plenty of opportunities again in 2026. Fantasy managers just shouldn't expect him to move the needle significantly.

On the surface, Matthews' second taste of the majors didn't go that much better than the first. But upon closer examination, there was a lot to like about his 16-start performance, which sets him up to be a full-time starter for the rebuilding Twins. Matthews' ERA-FIP differential was the third widest (in the wrong direction) among pitchers with at least as many as his 79 1/3 innings, and he earned above-average grades for his velocity, control and ability to suppress hard contact. He's a sleeper among pitchers available in the latter rounds of mixed-league drafts, especially if he's throwing well during spring training.

Shifted to the bullpen full-time to begin 2025, Detmers added two ticks to his average fastball velocity and, after some early struggles, thrived in his new role. Over his final 49 appearances, he had a 2.19 ERA, three saves, 13 holds and a 33.5% strikeout rate. The Angels, perhaps seeing his improved stuff and control -- as well as considering his past history as a starter -- entered spring training planning to have him back in their rotation for 2026. With that move, Detmers' fantasy upside increases, but he’ll warrant careful examination to see whether he can first maintain his 2025 gains.

Reliever ERAs can be deceptive, and Hoffman was a clear example of that for several years. He beat his estimators in four straight seasons, running an ERA well below what his peripherals suggested. It led to expectations of regression, and his 4.37 ERA last year was his highest since 2021. Even so, a 3.21 SIERA suggests the results were inflated. While there was some skills slippage, potentially tied to a move into the AL East, the biggest problem was a sharp spike in home runs, as his 1.99 HR/9 ranked among the league's worst. Hoffman still recorded a career-high 33 saves, fourth most in baseball, but frequent long balls are a quick way to lose managerial trust, particularly in high-leverage spots like the postseason. He remains part of Toronto's saves picture, but opportunities will have to be earned, and limiting home runs will be critical.

Vaughn got off to a horrific start to 2025 with the White Sox, ultimately earning himself a ticket back to Triple-A ball, then a trade to the Brewers. One Rhys Hoskins injury later and Vaughn was playing regularly in Milwaukee, generating a top-50 fantasy point total among hitters from his July 7 recall forward. Greater patience and a small adjustment to his swing contributed and, while regression is sure to strike in 2026, those changes and Milwaukee’s HR-friendly home environment should help keep Vaughn in the fantasy-relevant tier. He’s a good corner infielder for traditional mixed-league play.

Miller's skill set should be especially appealing in roto play, as he's a speedy prospect who swiped 59 bases in 116 games between Double-A Reading and Triple-A Lehigh Valley last season. Scouts see him developing more power upside from the 14 homers and .433 slugging percentage he had there. He's a shortstop for now, but might figure into the Phillies' third base plans at some point during the year, making him a worthy dynasty pick.

The move from Cincinnati to Kansas City proved tough on India in 2025. He finished the campaign with the worst offensive numbers of his career, including a .669 OPS and nine homers in 567 PA, limping to a .194 average in the second half. The Royals are blaming his struggles partially on India moving around between second base, left field and third base, and they plan on leaving him at the keystone in 2026. Perhaps more stability in his defensive role will help his offensive production, but India is looking more and more like a player who peaked right away upon arrival in 2021 when he won NL Rookie of the Year. Any sort of bounce-back effort will likely come without steals since that aspect of his game completely vanished in his first season with the Royals.

Meadows was limited to 58 games in 2025 due to arm and quadriceps injuries, but it wasn't much better when he was healthy with a .215/.291/.300 slash line. He posted just four home runs and four steals in 213 plate appearances, with a 26.3 percent strikeout rate being the worst of his three MLB campaigns. Meadows illustrated his power and speed potential in 2024 with nine home runs and nine stolen bases over 82 games, but he's yet to show that he can consistently perform at that level in the majors. His reliable defense in center field should help him to maintain playing time, but the Tigers may not wait too long to test their other options if his offensive struggles carry over into 2026. Beyond that, there's also the question of whether or not Meadows can stay healthy.

Liberatore finally got a full-season look as a starter for the Cardinals, and he was a solid rotation piece with a 4.21 ERA, 1.31 WHIP and 122:40 K:BB across 151.2 innings. He fared better early in the season and had a 3.70 ERA at the end of June, but the career-high workload may have caught up with him a bit during the second half. He'll get plenty of runway to start in 2026 with the Cardinals finally going all-in on a rebuild, and he should be a bit more reliable in his second year as a full-time MLB starter, with a 6.2 percent walk rate giving him a strong base. However, Liberatore did give up a fair amount of hard contact and doesn't have much strikeout upside, so his ceiling is limited.

Patrick essentially came out of nowhere in 2025, delivering a 3.53 ERA, 1.28 WHIP and 127:40 K:BB across 119.2 innings for the Brewers as a rookie. He had some stints at Triple-A during the second half once Milwaukee's rotation got healthy, but he worked out of the bullpen during the closing stretch of the regular season and the playoffs. A 3-8 record was the only real blemish against him, as wins were difficult to come by at times with just six of his 23 starts lasting at least six innings. Patrick would have some fantasy upside if he can crack Milwaukee's starting unit in 2026, but he isn't guaranteed to be a regular member given the plethora of options the club has to round out the rotation.

After receiving his first taste of the majors in 2024 with two starts, Waldrep spent the 2025 campaign with Triple-A Gwinnett before making his season debut for Atlanta in early August. The right-hander was one of the best starting pitchers in baseball down the stretch, going 6-1 with a 2.88 ERA, 1.19 WHIP and 55:22 K:BB in 56.1 innings across 10 appearances, and he gave up more than three runs in just one of those outings. Unfortunately, the 2023 first-round pick underwent surgery in February to remove loose bodies from his right elbow, likely shelving him for at least the first two months of the season. Waldrep has a high ceiling and could be Atlanta's next home-grown, standout starter, once he's healthy enough to return.

Keith has not exactly performed to the expectations set forth by his 2023 minor-league campaign, but he was more productive during his sophomore season at the big-league level in 2025. Oftentimes, players struggle to avoid the sophomore slump, yet Keith showed a more discernible eye at the plate while hitting with more power, so he appears well positioned to take another step forward in 2026. Keith's aforementioned plate discipline makes him a strong candidate to bat leadoff, which would help push his volume up. However, Keith will need to show he can do more against lefties than he has thus far in his career, because his .610 OPS against them in two seasons invites a platoon situation. His contract makes him a regular player in the lineup; what he does against lefties in 2026 will dictate whether he is promoted to an everyday role.

A ruptured patella tendon ended Casas’ 2025 in early May, ending what was a disappointing season only shortly after it began, and threatens to cut into the opening weeks and possibly months of 2026. The Red Sox, reacting to this, acquired Willson Contreras to handle first base, meaning Casas will have to fight for at-bats between first base and DH if he’s to recapture what had previously been massive power upside. Entering the year, Casas is one of the riskiest picks around and he’s better left to deep mixed or AL-only drafts until we get more definitive word on his health.

Bello began the 2025 campaign on the injured list with a shoulder issue but returned to make 29 appearances (28 starts) for the Red Sox during the regular season before adding an abbreviated start in the wild-card round. While he put together his best season ever on the surface with a 3.35 ERA and 1.24 WHIP over 166.2 innings, the skills were largely similar to prior years, indicating good fortune over legitimate growth. Bello's game is predicated on keeping the ball on the ground with his sinker over the swing-and-miss, and that makes him subject to the whims of variance. Still just 26 years old to begin the 2026 season, Bello should be viewed as a detriment to WHIP, but he is at least a capable innings eater for Boston, having reached 28 starts and 157-plus innings each of the last three years.

The veteran southpaw logged a career-high 181.2 innings with the Mets in 2024 before crashing back to earth in 2025, as injuries sabotaged both workload and performance. While rehabbing an oblique strain, Manaea required a cortisone shot to combat a loose body in his left elbow, which delayed his season debut until July 13. From there, he largely struggled, allowing nearly two homers per nine. The strikeout and walk numbers were impressive, indicating the potential for a bounce-back season in the New York rotation, if healthy. The loose body has not been surgically removed but Manaea nonetheless said in November that he considers it a thing of the past, adding that he hopes to pitch the rest of his career without needing an operation on it.

Woods Richardson again served as a back-end starter for Minnesota in 2025, though at one point it looked as though he could be exiting the rotation after posting a 5.74 ERA in his first nine outings. The right-hander closed out the campaign with a 3.00 ERA, 1.06 WHIP and 68:29 K:BB in 69 frames across his final 14 appearances, posting a 5-1 record during that stretch. He improved his strikeout production to 8.6 K/9 but also gave out more free passes (3.7 BB/9). Woods Richardson has a higher floor but a lower ceiling than teammate Taj Bradley, and the two could be in competition for a spot in Minnesota's starting rotation during spring training.

O'Neill landed with the Orioles last winter on a three-year, $49.5 million contract, but the first season of that deal was a complete disaster. The veteran outfielder played in just 54 games due to shoulder and wrist injuries, which were just the latest in an extensive injury history. O'Neill was unproductive when available, delivering nine home runs with four steals, 26 RBI, 22 runs and a .684 OPS in 209 plate appearances. The underlying numbers indicate O'Neill had some unfortunate luck with a .218 BABIP, but that's only part of the equation here. He's played 100 games in a season just twice since making his MLB debut in 2018, as he's simply been unable to stay healthy for any considerable length of time. The Orioles don't seem like they'll be counting on the outfielder to fill an everyday role in 2026 following the offseason acquisitions of Taylor Ward and Pete Alonso, and a more niche role like that could help O'Neill to stay healthy, albeit with an obvious hit to his volume.

The sinkerballer almost made pitching in Cincinnati look easy in his first season with the Reds in 2025, posting a 3.29 ERA and 1.11 WHIP over 90.1 innings at Great American Ball Park. He was not as fortunate on the road, but Singer finished with 14 wins and 15 quality starts, providing much-needed stability at the back of the rotation for manager Terry Francona. It was a situation where the piece fit exactly as intended for the team, though there is little in the numbers to suggest another level could be lurking underneath the surface with Singer at 29 years old. While he generally keeps the ball in the park, the strikeout rate is modest. Many will want to avoid tough matchups at home even with his success last season, as the park can exacerbate the bad days.

Giolito’s 2025 return from an internal brace surgery looked like a win for his on-field and fantasy teams, as he posted his lowest ERA in six years, but even a cursory glance under the hood reveals troubling trends. His strikeout rate (19.7%) dipped to its lowest number in seven years, his Statcast expected ERA was 5.06, and he finished the year on the shelf, missing the Red Sox’s Wild Card Series due to an elbow injury. Giolito lingered on the free-agent market deep into the winter, raising further concerns as he enters his age-31 season. If he lands in a good spot and opens spring training as a favorite for a rotation spot, he can be a matchups play or volume-oriented points-league late rounder. However, his prior lofty ceiling is in his past.

Littell’s pinpoint control makes up for his otherwise lackluster stuff, as over the last two seasons combined, he has an ERA (3.73) more than a third of a run lower than league average, despite a strikeout rate (19.2%) that’s more than 3% worse than average. He should again serve as a reliable MLB fourth starter, racking up useful innings for points-based fantasy teams, though he’s a difficult pitcher to stream because of his relatively balanced splits against good and bad opponents. If he lands in the right place, Littell can effectively round out your fantasy staff in deeper leagues.

Taillon averaged 30 starts per season over the prior four years but was limited to 23 last season after two second-half IL stints for a right calf strain and a left groin strain. Despite the missed time, he posted a sub-4.00 ERA for the third time in four seasons, even as his estimators have sat nearly a run higher the past two years. His strikeout rate has generally declined, though he showed a modest rebound compared to 2024, while his control remains near elite and his home-run rate tends to run high. In a retro draft, where players are selected based on that season's statistics, Taillon would have been a decent pick in three of the past four years. Looking ahead, the combination of modest strikeouts, home run vulnerability and emerging durability questions makes him a volatile option.

Rodriguez did not make an appearance at any level in 2025. The right-hander first received a cortisone shot in March to treat elbow inflammation before suffering a lat strain in April. He was eyeing a return before the break but was shut down again in July with renewed elbow discomfort, a setback which eventually led to debridement surgery. The baseball world let out a collective groan when the Orioles subsequently shipped Rodriguez to the Angels in exchange for Taylor Ward, as many read it as an indictment of Rodriguez's arm health. GM Perry Minasian said after the move that he examined the medicals and gained confidence that Rodriguez will be over his problems in 2026. It's difficult to trust, but Rodriguez is a former top prospect who showed a high level in 2024 before the lost season.

Ruiz's skills are closer to those of a reserve infielder. Few players, regardless of position, put the ball in play more, but he does so with very little authority. In prior seasons he leaned flyball, which supported modest power, but last year he hit grounders just under half the time, and as one of the slowest runners in the league he didn't beat many out. In late June, Ruiz was hit in the head by a line drive while in the dugout and missed the rest of the season on the concussion IL, though he's expected to be cleared by camp. A long-term contract should keep him in the mix, but the Nationals acquired Harry Ford to compete with Ruiz for time behind the plate.

Philadelphia did everything possible to show that Castellanos was not in the plans for 2026, and released him just before spring training. The Padres picked him up shortly afterward, with the idea that he'd compete for platoon at-bats between right field, first base and DH. Castellanos' new home should allow him to at least hit homers and drive in runs, but the skills decline here is real, so tread carefully.

Benintendi's time on the South Side has been forgettable, as he's been essentially a replacement-level player in all three years with the club. The left fielder began 2025 with an Opening Day homer but hit the injured list less than two weeks into the season with an adductor strain. He made a second trip to the IL in May with a calf strain, and a third at the end campaign with Achilles tendinitis. Benintendi managed to reach 20 homers for the second consecutive season despite all the missed time, but he hit .240 as his move to add flyballs in recent years has been a severe detriment to his batting average. Even the White Sox don't play him every single day, often shielding him from lefties. Benintendi will remain part of the regular lineup versus right-handed pitching as the club runs out the clock on his remaining two years under contract.

Rea transitioned from the Brewers to the Cubs in 2025 and posted a career-best 3.95 ERA with a 1.25 WHIP and 127:44 K:BB across 159.1 innings. He started in 27 of his 32 appearances and continues to provide value as a back-end starter, though his fantasy upside is limited given his 7.2 K/9 the past two seasons. Rea could work as more of a swingman for Chicago in 2026, though he should have a strong chance of opening the season in the rotation with Justin Steele expected to be unavailable for the first month or two of 2026 while rehabbing from elbow surgery.

After a pair of so-so seasons for the Pirates (2020-21), followed by three nondescript seasons in Japan (2022-24), Ponce moved to the Korea Baseball Organization for 2025 and immediately flourished. Thanks to his adding a couple notches of velocity to his fastball while introducing a kick-change, he set the KBO single-season record for strikeouts (252) and won the league's Choi Dong-won Award (their Cy Young equivalent). Ponce returns to MLB with the Blue Jays, whose focus on optimizing pitchers' repertoires was exhibited on the national stage last October, meaning he's a good fit to his new surroundings. Pitchers returning from overseas don't often approach their statistical levels there -- scouts liken KBO competition to our Double-A ball -- but he could at least serve as a volume-oriented matchups play or back-of-a-staff mixed-league pick.

Pfaadt didn't pitch as poorly as his 5.25 ERA indicates, but getting back on track will require more than regression. His 4.01 xFIP and 4.12 SIERA paint a more encouraging picture, as a low 66.5 percent left-on-base rate inflated his ERA. At the same time, a sizable drop in his swinging-strike rate drove a sharp decline in strikeouts, and a modest reduction in his walk rate wasn't enough to counter it. Pfaadt adjusted his pitch mix by throwing fewer four-seam fastballs and sliders while adding a cutter and leaning more on his changeup and curve. Because his four-seamer and slider generate most of his swing-and-miss, the shift coincided with a loss of dominance. His 18.8 strikeout-minus-walk percentage from the prior season supported optimism, but the 14.3 percent mark in 2025 is concerning heading into 2026.

The Blue Jays keep stocking rotational depth, re-signing the future hall-of-famer at the end of February for a fraction of what he signed for last year. While Scherzer is coming off one of his worst seasons and is an injury risk who has fallen short of 20 starts in back-to-back years, he still has enough moxie to help fantasy managers on a matchups basis. AL-only managers can regard him a late rounder, but in standard formats, seek those games against weaker lineups or in road pitching friendly parks.

Kremer surpassed 170 innings for the second time in three seasons. His ERA was its highest during that span, though his estimators were the lowest. Kremer's modest strikeout rate leads to more variance than more dominant arms, but he shows solid control and command to help keep his ratios around league average. In 2022 and 2024, he failed to reach 130 innings, so he cannot be counted on for a full season. The AL East is not an ideal division for streamers, but the Orioles have fortified their offense with Pete Alonso and strengthened their bullpen with Ryan Helsley, making Kremer an option for favorable matchups in deeper formats.

Signed last winter to the largest guaranteed deal in Athletics franchise history, Severino threw six scoreless innings in Seattle on Opening Day before a harsh introduction to Sutter Health Park. The veteran right-hander struggled to a 6.01 ERA and 1.53 WHIP in 15 starts at home in 2025, compared to a 3.02 ERA and 1.07 WHIP on the road. He couldn't find a pitch to put hitters away and saw his strikeout rate fall to a career-low 17.6 percent. The results improved overall down the stretch, and Severino still throws hard for a starting pitcher, averaging 96.1 mph on his four-seamer last season. However, the skills are not what they once were. This will feel like playing with fire so long as he's pitching in Sacramento.

Sears opened the 2025 campaign as a rotation regular for the A's but finished it as a spot starter for the Padres, who acquired him in the Mason Miller deal at the trade deadline. Sears has never offered a ton of fantasy upside, but he regressed across the board last season with a 5.04 ERA, 1.32 WHIP and 117:36 K:BB in 27 starts. He's served up at least 28 home runs each of the past three seasons and doesn't offer much strikeout potential. Sears profiles as a back-end innings eater more than anything else, but as a contending club the Padres aren't likely to give him such an extended leash if the troubles persist, which was evident in 2025 as he made just five big-league starts after being traded to San Diego.

A 2024 breakthrough reliever for the Twins, Sands' numbers took a step backwards last season, in large part because he was largely unlucky on batted balls. His ERA was nearly three-quarters of a run higher than Statcast's expected, though he also warrants some blame for having middling whiff and hard-hit rates, pointing to what were good-not-great underlying skills. As one of the team's more experienced relievers, however, Sands should be part of a spring closer competition, and we'll see whether saves or holds are his categorical target come Opening Day.

Lee put forth a second consecutive solid season in setup relief, his holds total swelling to a team-leading 19 in 2025. That he lowered his walk rate was a help, as that's one of the categorical fears among short relievers with the fly ball leaning he has (33.0 FB%). Lee should be one of the team's most trusted late-inning relievers again in 2026, though the addition of Robert Suarez, who should handle the eighth, might cap the lefty's holds ceiling around last year's total.

Povich's second major-league season in 2025 looked much like his rookie campaign, with a 5.21 ERA and 1.50 WHIP being quite similar, just with a larger workload. The left-hander improved both his strikeout and walk numbers (to 9.5 K/9 and 3.4 BB/9), but he surrendered too much hard contact for those improvements to matter. The Orioles have made some big splashes this offseason by signing Pete Alonso and trading for Shane Baz, and Zach Eflin is also back in the rotation mix. Since Baltimore is looking to immediately get back into playoff contention, Povich likely won't have much runway to iron out any troubles if he continues to struggle in the big leagues. The left-hander will likely need a strong showing during spring training to have a chance of cracking the Opening Day rotation, and even then there's no guarantee he sticks around for long.

Faucher, who inherited the Marlins' closer job over the final two months of 2024, served as the leader of a committee last season, putting forth effective-yet-unspectacular stats. He finished with 15 saves and a second straight year of a sub-3.30 ERA, though his 4.25 FIP suggests he's due for some regression. That the Marlins signed Pete Fairbanks to close probably pushes Faucher back into a primary setup role, from which he'd be more of a middling holds source. Consider him a matchups-driven reliever with a shot at some saves should Fairbanks' past injury issues resurface.

After absorbing a massive workload (100 IP combined between the regular season and postseason) during the Tigers' 2024 Cinderella playoff run, Holton's fantasy numbers (as well as his underlying metrics) took a small, predictable step backwards last year. Righties hit him harder, he surrendered more hard contact overall, and he surrendered a whopping 15 homers. Holton did manage 17 holds nevertheless, and he'll remain a key piece in A.J. Hinch's matchups-oriented bullpen. There should be enough opportunity here to keep Holton as a solid source of holds and K's for fantasy purposes.

Olson opened the season strong, delivering a 2.96 ERA and 1.17 WHIP with 51 strikeouts across 48.2 innings in nine starts. A bout of right ring finger inflammation sidelined him for nearly seven weeks, and after returning he lasted only four more starts before a right shoulder strain ended his year. Those final outings were less sharp, as he recorded a 3.60 ERA and 1.30 WHIP with 14 strikeouts in 20 innings. Olson has shown effectiveness when available, but durability remains an issue, as he's yet to exceed 22 starts or 113 innings. He's expected to open the year in the Tigers' rotation, and his per-start output plays well, particularly in formats with dedicated IL spots.

An 80-game suspension for PEDs cut out a chunk of Alvarado's 2025, but on either side of it, he exhibited top-shelf velocity and improved control, which led to him totaling seven saves and five holds in 28 total appearances. While the Phillies' midseason acquisition of Jhoan Duran probably locks Alvarado into their primary lefty specialist role, it's still one from which he can rack up many holds and strikeouts.

The Rangers could have themselves a future left-side-of-the-infield gem in Walcott, though his ascent to Arlington appears likely to wait until 2027 after February UCL surgery on his right elbow. For dynasty purposes, Walcott is a potential five-category roto standout who hit .255/.355/.386 with 10 homers and 32 steals in 124 games for Double-A Frisco last season. And before you say "well, that's hardly an eye-popping hitting line," bear in mind that he was once again one of the very youngest players at his competitive level. Walcott's injury and young age could cause a slow adjustment to the majors once he arrives, but his upside is so great, he's still a top-shelf dynasty stash.
